activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
Emma had told herself she would be calm about the community kitchen's chocolate night, and she was calm, which was why she had read three articles about tempering that afternoon and arrived fifteen minutes early with her hair already tied back. Mr. Leblanc, who ran the Thursday sessions out of the church basement kitchen, had put out blocks of dark chocolate and blocks of milk chocolate, a double boiler, and a thermometer with a small crack in its plastic casing. "You'll want to be gentle with that," he said, and Emma thought, obviously, because she was a calm and gentle person, as anyone who knew her would agree, except possibly her mother, whose opinion could be contextualized as the judgment of someone who had once seen Emma cry over a dropped meringue and never let it go.

Leanna was already there, claiming a corner of the steel counter and lining up molds in a way that suggested she had been a chocolate maker in a former life, or at least believed she had. Wesley showed up ten minutes late with a bag of pretzels he refused to explain. "For structure," was all he said, and he would not elaborate, and it hung over the evening like a small unexplained weather system.

The method Mr. Leblanc wanted them to try was seeding: melt most of the chocolate, cool it, then stir in chopped bits of already-tempered chocolate so their crystals would spread through the whole mass like rumors through a small school. The dark chocolate, he said, they would work at around thirty-one, thirty-two degrees. He said it once, while grinding coffee, and then left them to it, which Emma respected. She did not respect Wesley, who kept eating his seed chocolate and replacing it from the bag of pretzels, as though the two were interchangeable.

The dark batch went beautifully. Emma poured a test streak on the counter and watched it set with a satin sheen, and when she broke off a piece it made a sound like a tiny, decisive door closing. Leanna applauded with a spatula. Wesley said, "That's the snap," with the authority of a man who had heard about snapping secondhand.

Feeling generous, or possibly feeling superior, Emma moved on to the milk chocolate, and here she made a decision she would later describe to herself as reasonable, which is how you can tell someone is about to be wrong. She had read that tempering was about temperature, and she knew the number for dark, so she carried it over, cooling the milk chocolate toward thirty-one, thirty-two degrees, seeding it, stirring it, waiting for it to behave.

It did not behave. She streaked a test on the counter and it sat there, dull and greasy, refusing to set, like something that had decided not to participate in the evening at all. She streaked another. She put a third streak in the fridge, which Mr. Leblanc saw and raised one eyebrow at, an eyebrow that could only be described as scathing, though he said nothing, which was somehow worse. Emma stirred the bowl and told herself the chocolate was simply slow, the way some people are simply slow, and there was no reason to panic, and she was not panicking, she was stirring, vigorously, with slightly clenched teeth.

Leanna leaned over. "What temp is that?"

"Thirty-one and a half," Emma said, with the flat confidence of a hostage.

Leanna frowned at the thermometer, then at the bowl, then at her phone, which she had been consulting all night in a way Emma had assumed was social and now realized was research. "Hang on. That's the dark number. Look, this says milk chocolate is different. It's tempered to a lower working temperature, twenty-nine to thirty degrees. Something about the milk fat softening the cocoa butter." She turned the screen so Emma could see it, and Emma looked at the bowl of sludgy, streaked chocolate, and at her own beautiful dark batch sitting smugly beside it, and felt two ideas collide in her head: the part of her that wanted the one number to rule everything, and the part that had just watched that want fail in a concrete, greasy puddle on a church basement counter.

Was it cheating, she wondered, to let the milk fat have its own terms? It felt like cheating. It also felt like the difference between a chocolate that snapped and a chocolate that smeared on the fingers of whoever ate it, probably Wesley, who was at that moment eating a pretzel with the composure of a man unaware that any crisis existed.

She dragged the bowl back over the warm water, brought the temperature up until the streaks melted out, then cooled it slowly, watching the thermometer the way you watch a sleeping animal. Thirty-one. Thirty. Twenty-nine and a half. She seeded it again, stirred, streaked the counter, and waited, and this time the streak dulled at the edges first and then went quiet and glossy, and when she broke a corner off, it snapped. It actually snapped. Leanna grabbed her wrist and shook it. Wesley saluted with a pretzel.

Mr. Leblanc wandered over with his coffee and looked at the two finished batches, then at the thermometer lying in its puddle. "So what did we learn?" he asked.

Emma considered several answers, including a speech about humility, and a lie about having planned the whole thing as a demonstration. "Milk chocolate runs cooler," she said. "Twenty-nine, thirty. And the dark numbers don't transfer." She paused, because the next part she was less sure of. "I still don't know if I could do it again without the thermometer."

"Nobody can, the first ten times," Mr. Leblanc said, and drank his coffee.

Emma peeled her test streak off the counter in one unbroken ribbon and held it up to the fluorescent light.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
The test came back on a Tuesday, folded once, and Jake saw the red circle before he saw the mark. He had written his answer to the last question neatly, in the way that usually saved him: the antiderivative, the bar, the limits, then the subtraction, and at the very end, a small careful plus C. Nineteen out of twenty-five. The circle was around the plus C, and beside it Mr. He had written only, "Why?"

He took the test to the tutoring centre that evening because he had nowhere else to take it. His father's opinion of extra help was a kind of litotes, "not against it," which everyone understood to mean he thought Jake should manage on his own, and Jake had stopped arguing about the ride. He took the bus now, forty minutes past the shuttered car lot and the pawnshop with the guitar in the window, and arrived when the fluorescent lights had already gone that tired evening yellow.

Makayla was at the corner table, eating fries out of a paper sleeve and highlighting a biology sheet in three colours. "You look like somebody stole your bike," she said.

"Mr. He took off six marks." He sat down across from her and flattened the test on the table. "Not for getting it wrong. For getting it right with an extra letter."

She leaned over the page, chewing. She was better at calculus than she admitted, which Jake had long suspected was a strategy. "You put plus C on a definite integral," she said.

"So it's a constant. Constants are safe. You add constants to everything."

"You also subtract them from everything," Ashlynn said, dropping her bag on the third chair. She had come from swim practice, hair still wet, and she pulled the test toward her without asking. "Look, you do F of b minus F of a, right? That's what the bar means. So your C goes in on top and goes in on the bottom, and then..." She made a small gesture with two fingers diving into each other and canceling. "It doesn't survive the subtraction. It cancels out."

Jake looked at the page for a long moment. In his mind he ran it the way he ran everything, as a claim and then a check: if you add the same number twice, once to each value, and then subtract one from the other, that number vanishes. It did not matter what C was. It did not matter that he had written it. The answer underneath it was already complete. "So the marks weren't for the answer being wrong," he said slowly. "They were for me not knowing what kind of question I was answering."

"For you not knowing why your own answer works," Ashlynn said, which was a scathing thing to say gently, and she went back to wringing out her hair with a towel.

That night he sat at the kitchen counter and wrote Mr. He a message, because the centre had a portal and because saying it in person felt like too much stage. He typed it out and deleted it twice before it came out right.

Dear Mr. He, I looked at question 6 again. With a definite integral, the plus C gets added to F of b and also to F of a, and then one is subtracted from the other, so the C cancels out and the answer comes out the same without it. I put it there because I memorized that antiderivatives need a constant, but I never asked why. I'm not asking for the marks back. I'm asking if I can redo one problem on the board Thursday to show I understand it now. Jake.

He read it over. There was a part of him, the part that had carried a 78 average through three years of being told he was "not a math kid," that wanted to predicate his whole worth on those six marks, to treat them as a verdict rather than a correction. He had changed his mind about that somewhere between Ashlynn's wet hair and the bus ride home, though he could not have said exactly where. A correction was something you could use.

Mr. He's reply came before breakfast, four words and then a fifth. "Thursday. Board three. Prepared."

Thursday, the centre was quieter than usual. Makayla had claimed a table by the window and mouthed good luck at him without looking up. Mr. He handed Jake the marker, said only, "Same question," and stepped back with his arms folded.

Jake stood at board three. He wrote the integral, then the antiderivative, then the bar with its limits. He wrote F of b, and inside his head he watched the constant attach itself to it, harmless and identical. He wrote F of a the same way, the same silent C riding along. Then he subtracted, drew his line through both of them, one in the top term and one in the bottom, and let them vanish. The answer stood there plain, without any letter after it.

"Plus C," he said, turning around, "doesn't belong here. It cancels out."

Mr. He uncapped his pen and made a single small mark on the sheet in his hand. "Board four," he said. "Harder one."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
The tide was going out when Hudson spread his notes on the flat of a rock and weighted them with shells, because the wind at Annalise's family's beach house had already taken one page into the dunes. The test was Monday. It was Saturday. Somewhere behind them, her younger brother was burying Mr. Novák, the retired science teacher from three houses down, in sand with a seriousness that suggested neither of them thought it was a joke.

"You're doing it wrong," Annalise said, dropping onto the rock beside him. "You always study like the paper itself is going to be graded. Read it out loud. Explain it to me."

He looked at the graph first, the one Mr. Novák had photocopied from an old journal and taped to Hudson's door as a joke that turned out not to be a joke. The line climbed and climbed, decade after decade, a slow cruel staircase. "So carbon dioxide," Hudson began, "traps heat. Sunlight comes through, the Earth warms up, and it radiates infrared back out. The CO2 absorbs some of that infrared and sends it back down again. Like a blanket. But here's the thing." He paused, because he had reached the part that had bothered him since Tuesday. "Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air, and they don't do any of it. They're not greenhouse gases at all. The stuff that's almost all of the air lets the heat just pass through, and the trace stuff, the tiny fraction, is what holds it."

Annalise pulled her knees up. "That's backwards. If I were inventing an atmosphere, I'd postulate that the most common gases did the trapping. Ninety-nine percent versus a sliver. How does that even work?"

Hudson opened the textbook, and there it was, the sentence he'd read four times and disbelieved four times: molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation. Nitrogen was two nitrogens. Oxygen was two oxygens. Identical twins, both of them, and twins like that were invisible to heat. He had assumed the opposite for most of his life, had assumed that air, the whole heavy breathing mass of it, was the blanket. It wasn't. The blanket was the guest that barely existed.

"The book says two identical atoms," he said slowly. "That's the whole rule. So nitrogen and oxygen, being pairs of identical atoms, they can't absorb the infrared. It just goes straight past them."

"That's the weirdest thing you've told me all summer, and you once explained your uncle's postulate about the ghost light on the pier."

"That was different. That was hedonistic nonsense about vibes. This is real. Ninety-nine percent of the air is doing nothing, and we're changing the one percent that does everything." He tapped the graph. "This line. It's not hypothetical. It's a measurement, every year, for a century."

They sat with it a while. Down the beach, Mr. Novák had escaped the sand and was walking toward them, brushing himself off, and Hudson felt an old impulse to hide the notes, the way he'd hidden them in middle school when understanding things had made him a target. Annalise was watching him instead of the ocean. "Say the whole thing again," she said. "Like I'm your professor and I'm going to fail you if you skip a step." So he did, and he fumbled the order, and she interposed a question right where he fumbled, and he had to start over, and the second time it came out cleaner, and the third time he wasn't reading the book at all.

Mr. Novák settled onto the neighboring rock without asking, salt in his eyebrows. "I heard the word postulate from over there," he said. "Careful. That's how it starts."

"How what starts?"

"You'll find out in September." The old man nodded at the graph, at the climbing line, at the two of them arguing about the invisible fraction of the sky. He didn't explain anything further, which Hudson had come to understand was his way of saying he trusted them to get there.

The tide had gone out far enough to expose the sandbar, and Annalise's brother was already running for it, shouting something the wind took apart. Hudson folded his notes, and the page with the graph went into his back pocket, where the afternoon's damp would wrinkle it into something softer. Monday he would get the question right. That was certain, or near enough. The rest, the line still climbing, the ninety-nine percent standing there blameless while the sliver did the damage, the fact that he understood it now and understanding changed nothing by itself, he carried down the beach after her, barefoot on the cooling sand, and it weighed nothing at all, which was the strangest part.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
The bus pulled out of the lot at 3:12, and Taylor smoothed the folder on her knees for the fourth time. Her interview at Halloran's Pharmacy was at 4:30, close to the end of the route, which gave her forty minutes to learn how to seem like someone who deserved a register and a name tag. Alaa slid into the seat across the aisle and held out a hand, palm up, like she was collecting a toll.

"Phone," Alaa said. "You'll fidget with it otherwise."

Taylor surrendered it. "You're the interviewer. Ask me something."

"Why do you want this job?" Alaa asked, flat as a form.

"Because I need money and you're hiring." Taylor heard it leave her mouth and closed her eyes. "Okay. Again."

Emery leaned over the back of Alaa's seat, chin on his arms. "You're doing the stare thing. Stop doing the stare thing."

"I'm practicing eye contact."

"You're practicing glaring. There's a difference." He flipped open his psychology notebook, the one he'd been filling since September because he thought it made him look cerebral, and paged through it with one finger. "Here. This is from a real study, I copied it off the board. Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, 1999. People liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements." He tapped the margin. "So if the interviewer leans forward, you lean forward. If she tilts her head, you tilt yours. She likes you and doesn't know why."

Taylor took the notebook and read it twice. "That feels like cheating."

"It's a pharmacy, not a courtroom," Alaa said. "Nobody's getting a subpoena."

"I'm serious." Taylor handed the notebook back. "I'd be faking a whole person. They'd hire someone who doesn't exist."

"They'd hire someone who wants the job," Emery said. "Same thing."

The bus slowed for the middle school stop, and Ms. Gupta, who had been driving this route long enough to know everyone's stop without checking, glanced in the wide mirror above her. "You three arguing about posture?" Her voice carried over the engine without effort. "My niece does that. Copies how people sit. Swears it works."

"See," Emery said.

Taylor looked at her reflection in the window, darkening now that they'd turned onto the tree-lined stretch past the reservoir. She thought about her mother's interviews, the ones that hadn't worked out, the folding of her hands, the practiced nod. If a trick existed and she didn't use it, was that integrity or just being stubborn in a way nobody would ever notice or reward? She tried to hold both ideas without dropping either, and mostly managed.

"Again," she said to Alaa. "And lean back when you ask. Really lounge."

Alaa sprawled against the window, one arm over the seat. "Why do you want this job?"

Taylor lounged to match her, mirroring the arm, the angle, and found, oddly, that the words came easier from that loose slouch than they had upright. "Because I'm careful with things that aren't mine. I reorganized my grandmother's pill boxes every Sunday for two years, and she trusted me more than the pharmacy that kept messing up her dosages. I'd be good at the part of the job nobody brags about."

Alaa blinked. "Huh."

"What?"

"Nothing. That was just, like, an actual answer."

At the pharmacy strip mall stop, Taylor stood, then crouched again, suddenly unwilling to let the notebook's fact go unexamined. "But what if she notices? If she catches me copying her, doesn't the whole thing collapse? Doesn't it stigmatize me as, like, a manipulator?"

"Subtle," Emery said. "The word was subtle. If she notices, you did it wrong." The doors hissed. "Go."

Taylor stepped down onto the curb, folder under her arm. Through the tinted glass she saw Ms. Gupta's eyes in the mirror, watching her, and she straightened her shoulders the way the driver was straightening hers against the seat. Then she pushed open the door of Halloran's, where a woman in a green vest was already standing, arms crossed, waiting behind the counter.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
Isabelle claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the wobbly leg she steadied with a folded napkin each Tuesday. She opened her laptop, plugged it in, and pulled up the assignment description Ms. Lee had posted on Friday: build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Around her, the afternoon library went on in its ordinary way, a cart of returns squeaking past, sunlight moving slowly across the carpet, someone two tables over turning pages of a newspaper with great patience.

She had avoided the assignment all weekend, and she knew why. Her father wrote code for a living and had a habit of leaning over her shoulder, breathing approval or disappointment, and she had decided she would rather learn it badly on her own than well under his eye. So she was here, alone except for her own stubbornness, creating a file called Student.java and typing the skeleton Ms. Lee had shown them, a class with private fields for a name, an age, and a flag for whether the student was enrolled.

Haven dropped into the chair across from her, uninvited, holding a muffin with the paper half peeled. "Is that the Lee thing?" Haven asked, crumbs moving as she spoke. "Mariane finished hers Saturday. She says it took her an hour."

"Then Mariane can enjoy her hour," Isabelle said, and typed on. She wrote the private fields, then a constructor, then the getter methods, one for each field. It was oddly satisfying, like fitting cutlery into a drawer built to the right dimensions. She wrote a small test class next, a main method that would create a Student and print out what the getters returned.

The trouble arrived quietly. She had written the constructor to take the age and the enrolled flag but had forgotten the name entirely; it sat in her head as a parameter she meant to add and never did. She ran the test anyway, and the console printed a line where the name should have been, except it wasn't a name, and it wasn't empty either. It said null.

She stared at it. Haven leaned over, muffin suspended. "What's that supposed to be?"

"It's supposed to be a name," Isabelle said. "I never set it." She sat back and looked at the screen the way you look at a door that has opened onto a room you didn't know your house contained. The field had existed, and she had printed it, and Java had given her this word, null, without complaint, without error, as though it were a perfectly reasonable thing for a student to be called.

She made a second test, then a third, wanting to see the whole shape of it. She declared a number field she never set and printed it, and it came out 0. She declared a boolean and printed it, and it came out false. Fields you never set weren't garbage or blanks; they had these quiet defaults, 0 for numbers, false for booleans, null for object references like her name. It felt less like a rule she'd been taught and more like something she'd caught in the act, a fact of the language behaving exactly as it behaved when no one was watching. She wrote the three results on the napkin under the table leg's twin, in case the file didn't save.

"That's kind of creepy," Haven said, reading over her shoulder. "Like the computer pretending everything's fine."

Isabelle laughed, though she half agreed. Haven had a taste for dysphemism, calling the library "the mausoleum" and their school "the institution," and calling this null business "the computer lying to you." It wasn't lying, exactly. It was more like a neighbor who says nothing's wrong in a tone that tells you nothing's wrong only in the narrowest sense. Her father would have called sloppy coding pernicious, would have said errors that hide are worse than errors that shout, and for once she thought he might be right, which annoyed her, and which she decided she was allowed to think without telling him. She fixed the constructor, added the name parameter, ran the test again, and watched a real name print where null had been. Something about the smallness of it, the clean line of corrected output, began to invigorate her, and she opened the next exercise Ms. Lee had listed without letting herself weigh whether she wanted to.

Ms. Lee passed on her way to the reference desk, slowed, and glanced at the screen. "You found the defaults, I see," she said, tapping the napkin with its three neat entries. "Mariane found them Friday. Most people find them the hard way."

"This was the hard way," Isabelle said.

"Good," said Ms. Lee, and kept walking, and Isabelle pulled the keyboard toward her again.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Near Earth's surface a projectile's vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second, whether it is rising or falling.
story:
The air cannon at the science museum fired a tennis ball across the atrium every ninety seconds, and Layla had timed it so often on her phone that a security guard had begun to watch her instead of the ball. She was there because of the test. On Monday she had drawn a blank on the projectile question, Ms. Tremblay's red pen circling the empty space where her work should have been, and now it was Saturday and she had decided, with a private stubbornness she didn't try to explain to her mother, that she would understand it or spend the whole weekend failing.

Jeevan had come along because he said the planetarium was worth the bus fare, but he kept drifting back to where she stood at the rail, phone in hand, counting under her breath.

"You're doing homework at a museum," he said.

"I'm doing an experiment." She showed him the screen, a series of timestamps. "At home I threw a ball straight up and timed it, up and down. The ball slows on the way up at the same rate it speeds up coming down. Nine point eight metres per second, every second, rising or falling, same number. That's what my book says and I didn't believe it, so I came here."

The cannon thumped. The ball arced over a netted distance marked in metres, landing in a bin with a pneumatic sigh. Layla started her timer at the thump and stopped it at the landing: three seconds, give or take her thumb.

"So what's the question," Jeevan said. He leaned on the rail, blocking a small obstreperous boy who was trying to slap the button that triggered the cannon early. The boy retreated to harass the pendulum exhibit instead.

"The question is how fast it was going when it left, sideways, and I keep wanting to treat it like one motion. One arc, one speed." She drew the arc in the condensation of her water bottle with her fingertip. "But the marker on the floor says twenty-two metres, and nothing about the height. If it's in the air three seconds and the sideways part never changes, then sideways it's just distance over time. The vertical part is the part that changes, and it changes by that same nine point eight every second whether it's climbing or dropping."

Jeevan frowned at the ball, which an attendant was reloading. "That seems too easy."

"That's what's making me nervous." She wiped the arc off the bottle. She had spent the whole semester trying to subjugate physics to her own intuition, forcing the numbers to match what falling was supposed to feel like, and the intuition had won every argument and lost every mark. In the atrium, with the metres painted on the floor and the clock in her hand, the intuition had nothing left to say. Twenty-two metres in three seconds was a little over seven metres per second sideways, and that answer didn't care how the arc looked.

A voice behind them said, "You two are the first people all week to actually use the stop button." It was Renaud, from her physics class, holding a coffee he wasn't supposed to have indoors, grinning at them both. "I come here to escape projectile motion, and here it is, being projectile motion at me."

"Then help," Layla said. "Three seconds of flight. What was the vertical speed at launch?"

Renaud set the coffee down on the rail with the ceremony of someone who considered this his finest elocution on the subject of borrowed time. "If it loses nine point eight every second going up and it's in the air three seconds, then it spent half of that going up, roughly. Fifteen-ish metres per second, straight up, at the start." He paused. "Am I showing off? I studied this last night and I needed someone to tell."

"You're both doing it sideways and up separately," Layla said slowly. "The whole time. Like they're two different balls that happen to be the same ball."

"Separate the components," Renaud said, quoting the textbook in a flat voice, and then, less flatly, "which I never understood until just now, saying it out loud to a tennis ball."

The cannon thumped again. Layla timed it, thump to landing, and got a slightly different number than before, which meant either her thumb or the cannon was imperfect, and she wrote both times down without deciding which. Somewhere between the two measurements was the truth, and she could narrow it but probably not nail it, and she found she didn't mind. She looked at Jeevan, then at the painted metres, then at the ball resting in the bin.

"Again," she said, thumb over the timer. "Watch it climb this time. It's slowing the whole way up, same rate as the way down." The cannon loaded with its small mechanical breath.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
The portable classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and somebody's microwaved soup, and Austin got the good chair by accident, the one that didn't wobble, because he'd arrived early for the first time all semester. Writing club met on Thursdays at three, and Mr. Russo, who ran it, had given them their most ambitious assignment yet: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles that took up the same question. Austin had chosen two studies on whether later school start times improved student mood. Both had found improvement. That was the problem.

"It's not a comparison if they agree," Tristin said, dropping into the chair across from him and stealing a pretzel from Austin's bag without asking, which was their whole friendship in one gesture. "You need articles that fight."

"They do fight," Austin said. "Sort of. One of them says the effect is huge, the other says it's small but real."

Tristin's reply was laconic, a single syllable, "So?", delivered with a shrug that meant he considered the matter someone else's problem.

Austin spread the printouts on the table. The smaller article came from a boarding school that had shifted its start time by forty minutes; the researchers had surveyed thirty students before and after and reported a striking jump in self-rated mood. The second had drawn on a national sample of thirty thousand adolescents across dozens of districts, and its authors, in careful hedged language, found a modest improvement that they described as real but limited. He had read both twice, and he kept circling the same sentence in his notebook: which one do I believe?

Kathy arrived, hair still damp from swim practice, and leaned over the printouts. "Oh, the thirty-person one," she said, tapping it. "We just did this in stats. A result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a big one. Thirty thousand people, the estimate gets precise. Thirty people, it could be all over the place."

"That's it?" Austin said. "The big study just wins?"

"It's not a fight with a winner," Kathy said, already losing interest, scrolling her phone. "It's like, what each of them can actually claim."

Mr. Russo drifted past their table on his circuit of the room, saw the printouts, and asked only whether Austin had found his thesis. Austin said not yet, and Mr. Russo moved on, which felt less like neglect than like a door being held open. Austin stared at the two studies and felt something rearrange. The small study wasn't wrong exactly; it could only see coarsely. The large one saw finely and reported something smaller. Both had told the truth as they were able to see it.

He began drafting right there, in his cramped handwriting, on the back of a permission slip he was supposed to have returned two weeks ago. The review, he wrote, should hold both findings in view: the dramatic result from thirty students deserved caution rather than dismissal, and the modest result from thirty thousand deserved respect rather than triumph. The interesting question wasn't which article to believe but what each one could honestly claim, and how a reader weighing evidence might sit between them. He crossed out "might" and wrote "must," then crossed that out too, because must was the vocabulary of a sycophant to his own argument, flattering it into sounding stronger than it was.

"Read some," Tristin said, mouth full of pretzel, when Austin had gone quiet for ten minutes.

Austin read the middle paragraph aloud, the one where he argued that precision itself was a kind of finding, that the wide margin of error around the small study's dramatic number made it suggestive rather than decisive, while the large study's tight estimate made its modest claim hard to shake. His voice caught on the word "suggestive," which suddenly seemed too stylish, and he plowed through anyway.

"That's actually decent," Tristin said, sounding personally offended by the fact.

"It's not finished," Austin said. "I don't know how to end it. Whether later start times actually help, I mean. That part's still open."

"So say that."

The bell for the late bus sounded down the hall, a flat electronic tone that emptied half the room in seconds. Kathy gathered her bag and paused at the door long enough to say, "The honest papers are the ones that admit what they don't know," and then she was gone, which for Kathy was practically a speech. Austin sat in the good chair a moment longer, the wobbly ones all abandoned around him, and wrote a final line he was almost sure about: the evidence favors a small benefit, but how small, and for whom, the studies between them cannot yet say. He underlined nothing. He put the pen down and looked at the two printouts lying side by side, the thick one and the thin one, and turned off the lamp above the table.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Mark 2:27, Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath, answering critics of his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath.
story:
The reunion was at her grandmother's house, the one with the screened porch and the long table that unfolded to seat fourteen, and Brooklyn arrived holding a printout she had been carrying around folded in her back pocket for three days. She had a reason. On Friday, Ms. McKenzie had announced the topic for the interfaith debate tournament: whether an ancient religious rule could still bind people in modern life, and the rule her team had drawn was the Sabbath. Her partner was Samir, who was Muslim and had said, dryly, that he would bring his own material, thank you. Brooklyn had drawn the Christian side without knowing much about it beyond the folder of verses Ms. McKenzie had told them to collate before the weekend was out.

The printout came out at the table, between the potato salad and her uncle's story about a boat. She had marked it up in three colors. Her grandfather, two seats down, noticed the highlighter before he noticed the paper.

"Is that homework?" he said. "On a Sunday."

"Kind of." She flattened the page. "It's for debate. I have to argue whether Sabbath rules still apply now."

Her grandfather set down his fork. "Sunday is Sunday," he said. "That's not a thing you argue. That's a thing you keep."

"I'm not arguing against it," she said. "I'm arguing about it. There's a difference."

He said that in his day nobody scheduled anything on Sunday, and her mother made a sound like a kettle deciding not to whistle. Brooklyn knew the history from experience: her cousin's soccer league had moved its games to Sunday mornings that spring, and the grandfather had said the family should pull the cousin out. The parents had not pulled the cousin out. It had been a standing chill ever since, polite and unspoken, like a vestigial limb of some older, larger argument.

"Actually," Brooklyn said, and then stopped, because her cousin was eleven and sitting right there, picking at a roll. She changed direction. "Grandpa, can I read you something? It's one of the verses. Mark, chapter two, verse twenty-seven."

He folded his arms, which meant go ahead, and she read it. "The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath."

"That's Jesus," she said. "That's him saying it."

"Context," said her aunt from the end of the table, delighted.

"It's not me interpreting it," Brooklyn said. "It's the situation. He and his disciples were walking through a field on the Sabbath and the disciples were picking grain, and some critics saw them and objected, said you can't do that, it's work. And that's when he said it. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath." She put her finger on the printout to show she was not inventing any of it. "So the rule exists, in the text. But the text also says the rule is for people. People weren't made to serve the rule."

Her grandfather was quiet long enough that the cousin started chewing again.

"You know what that's called," he said finally. "Picking the verse that suits you."

"That's fair," Brooklyn said, and meant it. "That's actually the other side's whole case. Samir and I wrote it down. You can take that same sentence and use it both ways. If the Sabbath is made for man, then man gets to decide what it's for. Or, if it's made for man, then keeping it is good for man, and dropping it is like throwing away something given to you. Both readings come out of the same words."

"So which are you arguing?" her aunt asked.

"That's what I can't figure out." She turned the printout over, where her notes were. "In the actual story, Jesus doesn't say forget the Sabbath. He just says the disciples picking grain isn't the point. So the rule didn't vanish. It got reexplained. Which is what we do now anyway. Nobody here keeps it the way people kept it in Mark. Not even you, Grandpa. You drove here."

He started to say something about driving not being work, and she watched him arrive at the quagmire ahead: that once you started deciding what counted and what didn't, you were already doing the thing he said nobody should do, and there was no clean line where the deciding stopped being allowed. He didn't say any of that. He looked at the cousin instead.

"Does the league feed them lunch after?" he asked the cousin's mother.

"Sandwiches. Sometimes pizza."

He nodded slowly, twice, like a man signing something. "In my day we'd have gone home for lunch," he said. "But I suppose the sandwiches feed them just as well." Then he picked up his fork and pointed it at Brooklyn's page. "You're still not going to win arguing that the rule is nothing. It's not nothing."

"I know," she said. "That's not what we're arguing."

She slid the printout back into her pocket. On Monday she would sit across from Samir in the library and admit that she had a position now but not a clean one: the rule applied, and the rule bent, and the text itself was where the bending happened, and she could not prove where the bending ought to stop. Outside, the cousin was already kicking a ball against the porch screen, waiting for practice to start.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
The seat numbers were stamped in faded orange, and Jonathan's father had already claimed the aisle with the insouciant ease of a man who considered stadiums his natural habitat. Anne-Sophie sat on Jonathan's left, Mahdi beyond her, all three of them seventeen rows up behind the west basket, close enough to hear the sneakers squeal. In the third quarter the home team's shooting guard made five shots in a row, and the whole section came apart. Anne-Sophie was on her feet shouting that he was on fire, that he could not miss, that the coach should clear the floor and let him shoot until the rim surrendered.

Jonathan pulled her sleeve. "The hot hand isn't real," he said. "It's a famous thing. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985. They studied it and called it an illusion."

"Called what an illusion?" Mahdi leaned across Anne-Sophie, phone already out.

"The hot hand. The whole idea. People just see streaks in randomness."

His father turned around with a mouthful of peanut shells. "That kid's hot, I don't care what your professors say."

"They're not my professors, they're statisticians." Jonathan felt the old pleasure of knowing something the adults didn't, the small clean click of being right in public. Anne-Sophie was still standing, still shouting, and the guard missed his sixth shot badly, and Jonathan said "see" at exactly the moment the ball clanked off the back iron. His father laughed with his whole chest.

The guard made six of his next eight anyway, and the section roared at each one, and Jonathan got quieter. He could feel the argument slipping out of his hands the way a greased ball does, and he didn't like the feeling, because being right had always been his thing, the thing he could carry into a room. Mahdi kept scrolling, tongue between his teeth, the way he did when he was determined to win a debate on technicalities. "Jonathan," he said finally. "There's a reanalysis. Miller and Sanjurjo, 2018. They found a statistical flaw in the original study."

"Meaning what?"

"Evidence of streak shooting. Actual streaks." Mahdi held up the phone like a verdict. Anne-Sophie read over his shoulder and started laughing, and Jonathan's father demanded to know what was so funny, and for a moment everyone was talking at once about a study none of them had read, while forty thousand people below them watched a basketball game.

Anne-Sophie watched Jonathan more than she watched the court after that. She had known him since the year their families had shared a beach house, and she knew the specific stillness he got when a belief was being taken apart in front of him. His genealogy of arguments was usually so tidy: a fact, a source, a win. Now Mahdi was reading aloud from a small bright screen, and the guard was making his ninth shot, and Jonathan was nodding slowly, saying "okay" in a voice that had gone careful. She found she liked him better in that voice. It cost him something to use it, she could tell, and it made him less sure of himself and more present, and she didn't know yet which of those she was supposed to prefer.

"So I was wrong," Jonathan said. It came out flatter than he meant. "Or the 1985 people were wrong and I just repeated them."

"Both," Mahdi said cheerfully. "You reified it. You turned a study into a law of nature because it had names attached."

Anne-Sophie said, "But now you're doing it again with the 2018 one. That's my problem with you and Mahdi both. You each find a study and build a church around it."

Jonathan opened his mouth to argue and then closed it, because she had put her finger on something he couldn't answer yet: the possibility that certainty itself was the mistake, whichever paper it wore. Below them, out of a timeout, the coach kept the ball in the hot guard's hands, and the guard missed twice, then made a shot so difficult the arena seemed to inhale before it went in. Jonathan watched the man's face afterward, serene, no more confident after the make than after the misses, and wondered whether anyone in the building, statisticians included, actually knew what was happening inside that body at that moment.

In the last minute the home team led by two, and the guard, double-teamed, passed to the worst shooter on the floor, a big man who had not scored all night, and the big man shot it anyway. Anne-Sophie grabbed Jonathan's arm. The ball was still in the air when the buzzer began to sound.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
Laurence had chosen thermodynamics because it sounded unarguable. Enthalpy, the heat content of a system at constant pressure, did not care whether you believed in it, and after a semester of English class spent arguing about books she had half-read, she wanted a topic with the temperament of arithmetic. Her paper for Mr. Popal was supposed to have an argument, footnotes, a bibliography in a standard citation style, and she had assumed the hard part would be the science. She was wrong about that, though not until Thursday did she find out how.

The library after school had that end-of-day smell of warm dust and pencil shavings. Laurence spread her draft across two tables. Eleven sources: a chemistry textbook, three journal articles she had found through the school database, a government report on energy efficiency, an obsolescent encyclopedia from the reference shelf that Mr. Popal had told them they could use only if they admitted it was old. She had listed them in the order she had used them, because that was how she had experienced them, and it had not occurred to her that there was another way.

Cale dropped into the chair across from her with his own draft and a bag of chips he was not supposed to have in the library. He read upside down, which was a habit Laurence found show-offy until she realized he actually could do it. He frowned at her last page for a long time.

"Your bibliography's in the wrong order," he said.

"It's in the order I cited them."

"That's the problem." He turned the page toward himself, right side up, as though the issue could only be seen properly from that angle. "In Chicago, MLA and APA, the entries go alphabetically by the author's surname. Not in the order you used them. It doesn't matter which style you pick, they all do it that way."

Laurence looked at her list. The textbook was first because she had opened it first, in September, before she had known anything. The journal articles came later, and the old encyclopedia last, a kind of confession. Rearranging it felt like lying about how she had learned things, like presenting the finished maze instead of the wandering. But she got a pen and began writing surnames in the margin, sorting them like a deck of cards, and something about the alphabet's indifference to her personal history both annoyed and, she had to admit, slightly emancipated her. Her process was not the reader's problem.

Lola arrived at four with her own paper, on prison reform, and the three of them formed the loose club that Mr. Popal had suggested they form without ever calling it a club. Lola's argument was the opposite of Laurence's in spirit: where Laurence wanted to prove something about heat that was already true, Lola wanted to persuade people of something that was not yet true anywhere, and had to build it out of testimony and statistics. Laurence read Lola's draft and found the argument moving and the evidence thin. Lola read Laurence's and said it was solid but read like a filing cabinet.

They argued about it, low-voiced, while a librarian shelved books behind them. Lola said that a paper with no stakes was a report. Laurence said that a paper with no evidence was a wish. Cale ate his chips and said they were both right, which Laurence told him was not a position, and he said it was the only honest one available, which she could not immediately disprove.

It was nearly five when Lola, flipping back to Laurence's bibliography, stopped. "Wait," she said. "You cited twelve things in the text. There are only eleven entries."

Laurence counted the footnotes. Twelve. She counted the bibliography, which she had just alphabetized so carefully, and found the missing one near the bottom of her draft, in a footnote she had written at midnight two days before and never transferred to the list. It was a small article, a minor source, and part of her wanted to leave it out, because adding it meant redoing the alphabetical order she had just finished. She said so, out loud, as a joke. Neither of them laughed.

She added the entry. She resorted the list, the new author sliding in between two others whose names she now knew better than she knew some of her relatives'. Then she checked every footnote against the list, one by one, with her finger on the page, and found nothing else missing, and sat back with the feeling of having closed a door and heard the latch catch.

On Friday Mr. Popal returned drafts with comments in green pen, and on Laurence's last page, beside the alphabetized bibliography, he had written a single line: order correct, but you have cited in footnotes throughout, so you are in Chicago style, and your heading still says MLA. She read it twice. Cale, leaning over from the next desk, read it too, and she watched his face do something complicated, because his own paper, the one that had corrected her, said MLA at the top and had footnotes as well.

"We match," Laurence said, and handed him the green pen.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged 13 to 17 who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall.
story:
Lucas taped the schedule to the gym door at seven forty in the morning, before anyone else arrived, so it would be the first thing the team saw. He had spent two nights on it, graph paper and a pencil with a chewed eraser, blocking the week into days: sprint work Monday, ball control Wednesday, a full session Friday, and two days marked only with the word REST, circled twice. Below the grid he had written a warm-up, twenty minutes, the same one every day. He stepped back and looked at it, and it looked smaller on the door than it had in his notebook.

"You're the captain now," his father had said when the coach announced it, "so act like it," which was easy to say from a kitchen chair. Lucas was eighteen and had never planned anything larger than a birthday party for Norman in tenth grade, an event now remembered mainly for the fire alarm. What he wanted, and wanted badly, was for this season to be different from the last one, when Bently tore something in his knee in the second game and sat out eleven weeks, watching from the bench with his leg wrapped like a parcel.

Bently found him at his locker before first period. "I saw the paper," Bently said. "Twenty minutes of warm-up. Before we even touch a ball."

"The FIFA 11+," Lucas said. "That's what it's called."

"The FIFA what?"

"It's a warm-up program. It has a name." Lucas closed his locker. "Come to the gym at lunch and I'll show you the part I didn't fit on the door."

By lunch the gym smelled of floor wax and old sneakers, and Norman had dragged in three others, so there were five of them sitting on the bleachers, which was more than Lucas had expected and somehow harder. He had a folder, and inside the folder was a single printed page, and the page was really the whole of his argument. "I looked it up," he said, and immediately regretted the phrasing, because it made him sound like a student and he wanted to sound like a captain. "In 2008, in Norway, they ran a trial. Young female soccer players, thirteen to seventeen. The ones who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall."

Norman leaned forward with his elbows on his knees. "A third fewer. Than the ones who didn't do it?"

"That's what the trial found."

"What kind of injuries?"

"All of them. Overall, about a third fewer." Lucas held the page out, and Norman took it and read it slowly, moving his lips a little, and passed it along.

The third player, a boy who had skipped last Saturday's session without apology, said, "We're not girls, and we're not Norwegian," and a couple of them laughed, and Lucas felt the whole folder, the graph paper, the two circled words, begin to slide toward a morass of shrugs and excuses, the kind of non-decision where nothing is agreed and nothing is refused and everyone keeps doing exactly what they were doing. He also knew the kid had a point he couldn't answer. The trial was young women, that age, that sport. Whether it carried over to an impecunious boys' team in a school gym that couldn't afford proper mats, Lucas could not say, and he decided in the moment not to pretend otherwise.

"I can't promise it works the same for us," he said. "I can promise it's ten to twenty minutes and it might keep one of us off the bench for eleven weeks." He looked at Bently when he said it, and Bently looked back and then down at his own knee, and the laughing player looked away first. "The rest days are the other half. Bodies recuperate on rest days, not during practice. That part isn't from the trial, that's just how it works. You build on the days you skip."

Nobody said yes. But Norman stood up and said, "Show us the first bit then, since we're here," and Lucas opened the folder on the floor and started them on the running drills, easy ones, knees up, side to side, and by the time the bell rang there were seven of them, because two more had wandered in and stayed. The schedule still hung on the door, and on Friday Lucas would find out whether anyone came to the full session, and whether the player who laughed would show up at all. For now he jogged at the back of the line, watching their feet, counting them out loud.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
The fence behind first base was wrapped in honeysuckle, and by July the whole outfield smelled like it, sweet and a little rotten where the flowers dropped onto the warning track. Leah had joined the summer team in June mostly because Kathleen said it would be funny, and stayed because it turned out she could hit. Not every time. Not even most times. But some evenings the ball left her bat like it had somewhere to be, and those evenings were the reason she kept showing up at six o'clock with her glove smelling of leather and grass stain.

Yohan noticed before she did. He played second base badly and kept a notebook worse, pages of tally marks in mechanical pencil, and after a game in which Leah had gone four for four he sat on the bench unscrewing his water bottle and said, "That's the third time this month you've had back-to-back multi-hit games after starting cold the week before."

"I don't know what you're doing with that notebook," Kathleen said, "but it's creepy."

"It's data," Yohan said. "There's a whole argument about whether it means anything."

The coach had his own theory, which he delivered while hitting grounders to the infield: get your front foot down early, see the ball, trust your hands. Yohan, who trusted nothing he hadn't tested, cornered him by the batting cage one Tuesday. The argument carried across the diamond, audible even over the crack of the machine. The coach said the hot hand was a myth, that some psychologist had proved it decades ago, that people see patterns in coin flips. Yohan said that wasn't the whole story, and the coach said he didn't want to hear about economists during batting practice, and Yohan walked off toward the arboreal shade of the big oak past third base, notebook rolled in his fist.

Leah followed him, partly because she liked knowing how things worked and partly because the argument was about her. "What psychologist?" she asked.

"The nineteen eighty-five study," Yohan said. "They analyzed pro basketball players, looked at whether a made shot raised the chance of the next one, and found basically nothing. So for thirty years everybody said the hot hand doesn't exist." He thumbed the corner of a page. "But it turned out the way they counted was wrong. There was a statistical bias baked into it."

"What kind of bias?"

"The kind that makes streaks look smaller than they are. Which is a weird thing, honestly. Even in coin flips, if you only look at the flips that come after a heads, tails shows up more than you'd expect. Think about that for a second. It shouldn't feel true and it is." He looked at her, checking. "So in twenty eighteen, two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed the old analysis was flawed, and when they reworked the same data, the same data, they found evidence of streak shooting. The hot hand might be real after all."

Leah sat down in the grass. There was something in this that she couldn't leave alone, a small hinge in the world. "So the coach is quoting one paper and you're quoting a newer one."

"They're using the same numbers. That's the part I can't get over."

All week she turned it over, on the bus, in the shower, standing in left field while Kathleen pitched warm-up throws that arrived like apologies. The coach wasn't stupid; his whole system was built on repetition, on the belief that a swing grooved through a thousand reps would hold up under pressure. Yohan believed something almost identical, that a thousand observations would reveal the truth. Both of them trusted patterns. They just disagreed about which pattern, and the disagreement underpinning their argument was older and stranger than either of them had noticed: whether a person could be trusted to know what she was doing while she was doing it.

The next game was the worst of her season. She struck out twice looking, once swinging at a pitch that nearly hit her, and in her last at-bat she chopped a weak grounder and was thrown out by four steps. Walking back to the bench she felt the evening air cool against the sweat on her neck, and there was a small bathos in it, the grand saga of her hot streak ending with a slow roller to shortstop. She dropped her helmet on the rack. The coach told her to get her front foot down earlier. Yohan said nothing, which was somehow louder.

Afterward, under the oak, Kathleen eating sunflower seeds and spitting shells into the dirt, Leah asked Yohan what he'd written about her tonight. He opened the notebook to the last page, almost shyly. Four hitless at-bats, dated, and beneath them a running average that had barely moved.

"So which is it," Leah said. "Was I ever hot, or was it just the season finding its level?"

"That's the thing. The math can tell you streaks happen more than the old study said. It can't tell you which streaks are real and which are luck. Not for sure. Not for one person over one summer." He closed the notebook. "There's evidence, and then there's the specific evening you're standing in."

She thought about the honesty of that. She could hold both things at once, maybe: that the pattern in the data was real, that Miller and Sanjurjo had found it sleeping inside numbers collected thirty years before, and that it still left her alone in the batter's box with a ball coming at her face and no theorem to swing. Maybe, she thought, that was the point. Not to resolve it, but to know exactly where the knowing stopped.

The field lights buzzed on, moths already spiraling up into them. Kathleen threw her a seed pouch and Leah caught it one-handed without looking.

"Same time Thursday," Kathleen said.

"Same time Thursday," Leah said, and reached for her bat.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story:
The worksheet had six questions and the bus left at four thirty, and it was already twenty past three. Maxime stood in front of the mitochondria model, a plastic cross-section the size of a small car, its inner membrane folded into ridges that the label called cristae. Question four asked him to trace the path from glucose to ATP, and he had written nothing except his name, which he had then crossed out and rewritten because his hand was shaking from the cold walk from the parking lot.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Kimberly said. She leaned against the railing with her own worksheet blank, which made him feel marginally better. Alicia was three steps ahead, already reading the wall panels, her pen clicking in that rapid way she had when she was pretending not to be anxious.

"Glucose gets broken down," Maxime said. "That part I know. Glycolysis, then the Krebs cycle, then the electron transport chain. It's the last part I can't hold onto. Everyone keeps saying the chain makes ATP, but the chain is electrons. Electrons don't make anything. They just fall."

"Falling is a colloquialism," Alicia said without turning around. "They transfer. Ms. Tran would take marks off."

"She takes marks off for breathing." Their biology teacher was across the hall, stationed by the exit with her clipboard and her watch, collecting worksheets as students finished. Ms. Tran had told them on the bus that she wanted the sheets in her hand by four fifteen, no exceptions, because the driver refused to wait and the museum closed at five. Maxime checked the clock above the gift shop. Three twenty-six.

He walked around the model twice. The ridges of the inner membrane were strung with small yellow beads, and the label beside them said protons. On one side of the membrane the beads crowded thick, turbid as silt in a jar of pond water someone had shaken; on the other side they were sparse. Between the two sides, embedded in the membrane like a wheel in a lock gate, sat a rotating shape labeled ATP synthase. Maxime put his finger near it, not quite touching, the way you test a stove.

Kimberly came and stood beside him. "Okay," she said slowly. "My uncle has a farm up near Owen Sound. He's got this creek, and he dammed it, and behind the dam the water builds up and builds up, all that pressure on one side. Then there's a turbine in the dam wall, and when he opens it, the water pushes through and the turbine spins and charges a battery. Look at this." She pointed at the crowded yellow beads. "That's the water behind the dam. That wheel thing is the turbine."

"Then the protons push through the wheel," Maxime said, "and the wheel spins, and it sticks a phosphate onto ADP." He could see it whole now, the way you suddenly see the whole room when someone turns a lamp on. The electrons didn't make ATP. They pumped, and the pumping stacked the protons, and the stacked protons did the work. He looked at the panel to find what the process was called, because there had to be a name, there was always a name.

"Chemiosmosis," Alicia read off the wall, tapping the heading. "It's got a whole panel. Some guy named Peter Mitchell proposed it in 1961, that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, and he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1978 for it. Nineteen seventy-eight. Seventeen years before anybody believed him enough to give him a medal."

"People laughed at him for a decade," Kimberly said. "My uncle says everybody laughed at his dam too, until the lights came on."

Maxime wrote fast, printing small to fit the whole chain into the box beside question four, glucose to pyruvate to the cycle to the gradient to the wheel. His pen ran dry on the last word and Alicia handed him hers without being asked, which was the kind of thing that made her easier to be around than most people. He finished at four eleven and carried the sheet across the hall, warm with the pleasure of a thing understood, and Ms. Tran took it from him and squared it against her clipboard.

"Question four was the bonus," she said, checking her watch. "Question one is the graded one." She turned the sheet so he could see it. Question one: Compare and contrast this process with the one occurring in the plant cells displayed in the greenhouse wing, which the map showed at the far end of the building, past the gift shop, through a corridor Maxime had not yet entered.

The clock over the gift shop read four thirteen.

"Run," Kimberly said.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Koen's arm until he winced, and Isabelle watched the numbers climb on the classroom monitor the way you watch a stranger's luggage go around an airport carousel, waiting for something to be yours. Mr. Sow had set up four stations in the biology lab for the unit on cardiovascular health, and by Friday each of them had to be able to take a reading, interpret it, and explain to a panel of younger students how diet and exercise could change it. That was the deadline. Isabelle had a second one that nobody at school knew about.

The numbers settled: 118 over 76. "Textbook," Lina said from the next stool, reading over Isabelle's shoulder. Koen rolled down his sleeve, pleased with himself, as though he had personally authored his own arteries.

Isabelle's grandfather had a machine at home, a grey box with an arm cuff that hummed with what seemed almost a sentience, blinking at him while it squeezed. Last Sunday, while he made tea, she had flipped through the log he kept beside it, columns of dates and readings in his small upright handwriting. Saturday's entry said 134 over 84. When he came back in and asked what she was smirking at, she had prevaricated, telling him she was looking at the crossword on the opposite page, because she didn't know what the numbers meant and didn't want to sound ignorant about something that might matter.

In the lab, Mr. Sow circulated without explaining much, which was his way. He'd taped a printed chart to the whiteboard, the 2017 American guideline, and told them only, "It's all there. Read it like a map, not a verdict." Isabelle stood in front of it while Lina pumped the cuff on a practice arm. The chart's bands were precise. Under the 2017 American guideline, a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89, fell in a labelled range. She ran her finger down the column and said, half to Lina, half to herself, "Stage 1 hypertension."

"So 134 over 84 would be that," Lina said. "Either number can put you there, not just both together."

Isabelle's stomach tightened. Saturday's entry. One number, and then the other, both of them sitting comfortably inside that band. She thought of her grandfather's log stretching back months, entry after entry, while she had sat at his kitchen table prevaricating about crosswords. The clinic closed at five, and her mother would be home from work at half four, which gave Isabelle exactly one window to say something out loud.

She tried to rehearse it on Koen, who had volunteered to be the audience for her panel talk. "Diet and exercise lower readings over time," she began, "so someone whose numbers fall in that range can often bring them down, but they still shouldn't just decide that themselves." Her explanation of salt and walking was competent, she supposed, but her mind kept sliding toward her grandfather's kitchen, the tea going cold, the log with its patient columns. When Koen asked whether she was okay, she said she was fine, and the answer sounded specious even to her, a smooth little coin with nothing behind it.

At half past four she found her mother in the hallway, keys still in hand, and said the whole thing in one breath: the log, the numbers, the chart, stage 1 hypertension, 134 over 84, she thought he should see the doctor, she was sorry she hadn't said something on Sunday. Her mother stood very still, coat half off one shoulder.

"He already did," her mother said. "Three weeks ago. He's on medication, he's walking every morning with the Hendersons, he asked me not to make a thing of it." She hung the coat over the banister and looked at Isabelle for a long moment. "But he never told me he was writing the numbers down in that book. He kept a log for his doctor and hid it from me."

Isabelle thought of the grey box humming on the sideboard, its single patient eye. "Can I see it again on Sunday?" she asked. "The log, I mean."

Her mother picked up the phone. "Grandpa," she said, turning away. "Your granddaughter has been reading your blood pressure book."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
Jayden spread the printout on the kitchen table and weighted its corners with his mother's teacups, since she was on nights and would not need them until morning. The graph showed carbon dioxide climbing in a jagged line across a century, and the assignment was to explain it to Ms. Bouchard's class on Thursday, in plain language, as if the audience had never heard of it. He had written half a paragraph and deleted it three times. The line kept rising, and he kept feeling like he was lying, though he could not have said about what.

Usman came over after his shift, smelling of the fryer at the restaurant, and dropped into the chair opposite with the loose, generous sprawl of someone who wanted to be entertained. "Tell me the speech," he said, chin on his fists. "Blake told me you're doing the gases thing. Make it funny. If you get them laughing in the first ten seconds, they'll forgive you anything after." That was Usman's theory of everything, and it had carried him through two years of class presentations and one disastrous talent show, so Jayden could not dismiss it outright.

"It's not funny," Jayden said. "It's a graph."

"Everything's funny if you commit." Usman tapped the paper. "Go on. First line."

Jayden said the earth absorbs sunlight and sends heat back out as infrared radiation, and that certain gases in the air hold on to some of that heat, and Usman yawned so widely his jaw clicked. "See, you lost me at radiation. What gases? Why those?"

That was the question, and Jayden did not have an answer. He had the graph, and he had the phrase greenhouse gases, which everyone said the way they said weather, as if it were self-evident. He went upstairs for his laptop and came back down searching, expecting to find something recent, some satellite era consensus, some modern idea his report could lean on.

What he found stopped him with his hand still on the trackpad. In 1859, a physicist named John Tyndall had begun laboratory experiments measuring how different gases absorb infrared heat. Not modeling, not guessing. He had built apparatus, measured it. And what he found was that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb infrared heat, while nitrogen and oxygen do not. Jayden read the sentence twice. Nitrogen and oxygen were most of the air, nearly all of it, and they did nothing. The whole argument of his report, the thing he had assumed was an invention of his own century, had been sitting in a laboratory a hundred and sixty years before he was born.

"You look weird," Usman said.

"This guy figured it out in 1859. Before cars. Before the graph even starts."

Usman leaned over to look at the screen, and for a moment his face did the thing Jayden envied, openness without defence. Then he pulled back. "So it's old news. Great, that's your joke. 'The Victorians called it, folks.' I'm telling you, lead with that, you've got them."

Jayden looked at the graph again, at the line going up and up, and at Usman, who wanted a laugh the way other people wanted air, and he understood they were making two different reports about the same world. He had been trying to compartmentalize it, the funny version and the true one, keeping them in separate drawers, and the trouble was that the drawers kept leaking into each other. The gases did not care about delivery. The line on the page did not care about anything.

He tried the first minute out loud anyway, with Usman as the audience, and when he got to the part about Tyndall he watched his friend's eyes drift to the window, to the streetlight, to his phone on the table. Usman was not stupid; that was what made it sting. He just wanted something from Thursday that Jayden could not give him, a performance, and Jayden wanted something Usman found noxious, which was to stand in front of thirty people and say a hard thing slowly, with no armour on.

He drove Usman home at eleven, and they argued the whole way, mildly, the way friends argue when nothing is actually wrong. "You could do both," Usman said at the curb. "Open with Tyndall, get the laugh, then do your serious bit. Nobody's asking you to be a monk."

"Maybe," Jayden said, though he suspected that standing up there with a joke in his pocket was its own kind of dishonesty, a small purchase of safety paid for out of the truth's account. He could not prove that, either. Ms. Bouchard would probably tell him rectitude was not a public speaking strategy, if he ever used that word near her, which he would not.

Back home he sat at the table with the teacups still holding down the corners of the world. He wrote one sentence at the top of a fresh page. In 1859, a man measured the air itself and found that some of it holds heat and some of it lets it go. He read it aloud to the empty kitchen, and the line on the graph went on rising, past the edge of the paper, into the part nobody had drawn yet.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
The line at the middle school gymnasium moved in short, obedient shuffles, and Jade counted the people ahead of her: eleven, then nine, then eight. She had her registration card in her jacket pocket, folded once, and she kept touching it the way you touch a screen door to check whether the wind has caught it. Behind her, Ann was reading the sample ballot aloud in a low voice, impervious to the looks this earned from the woman in the green coat.

"You're doing the school board one, right?" Ann said. "Because my mom says the school board is the only race that actually touches your life, and everything else is theater."

"My grandmother says the opposite," Jade said. "She says the small races are how the big ones get bought."

"That's cheerful."

Ammar had been in line since six-forty and had already voted, but he had come back to stand with them, which Jade thought was either loyalty or the fact that his mother worked the sign-in table and he had nowhere better to be. He held out a paper cup of bad coffee as an offering. "Careful," he said. "It's for epicures only. I put three sugars in."

"Meaning it's not for epicures at all."

"Meaning it's for people who want to believe they're epicures." He grinned, then turned serious the way he did when he had been saving something. "Did you know there was a time when you couldn't do this at eighteen? Like, legally couldn't."

Jade said she had half known that, some vague picture of soldiers and protests, and then admitted she hadn't known it in any way that counted. Ammar nodded toward the far end of the gym, where a man with a clipboard was helping an old voter find her precinct table. "Mr. Cohen's here," he said. "Ask him. He loves this stuff, he'll talk until they close the polls."

They found him at the bake-sale table the PTA had set up beside the bleachers, selling muffins with the patience of someone who had done this for decades. When Jade asked, he didn't lecture. He only said, "Ask your grandmother tonight how old she was the first time she voted. Then look up the amendment that changed it." He took her dollar and gave her a corn muffin she hadn't wanted.

Her grandmother called during lunch, before Jade got to the gym, which was why the day had this shape at all. "I was twenty-one," her grandmother had said, "and your great-uncle was twenty-two, and we both thought that was just how it was. You kids get it at eighteen now, and you don't even know it was a gift." Jade had asked what she meant and her grandmother had said, "The amendment, sweetheart. Somebody changed it. You go look it up and tell me what you find." She had said it like a dare, and Jade, sitting on her bed with the phone on speaker, had looked it up.

The 26th Amendment. It set the voting age at eighteen, and it was ratified in 1971, and it had taken about three months, which made it faster than any other amendment ever. Jade had read the sentence twice, then a third time, because three months seemed impossible for a country that argued about everything. Laws about stop signs took longer than that. She tried to titrate her amazement against her suspicion, the way her chemistry teacher had taught her with the burette, adding one drop of doubt at a time, but the fact held. She texted Ammar, and Ammar had apparently texted his mother, and somehow the whole morning had become about it.

Now, at the front of the line, Jade gave her name to the poll worker, signed the book with a pen on a beaded chain, and carried her ballot to a booth with a curtain that smelled like chalk dust. The felt-tip pen hovered. Ann's mother said the school board was everything; her grandmother said money moved upward, from the small races to the big ones; Mr. Cohen had refused to say anything at all, just smiled and sold muffins. Both things could be true, she thought. A person could believe the local race mattered and still know it mattered to people with checkbooks.
