She filled in the school board bubble, then the county one, then paused at the state race for a long moment before filling that in too, and she did not feel settled, exactly, but she felt like someone who had at least looked at both sides of the door before walking through it.

She fed the ballot into the machine, and it made a sound like a stamp, like something official had happened to her. Outside, the October light was flat and bright on the parking lot. Ann was already arguing with Ammar about whether they had time for the diner before first period, and Ammar was saying his mother wanted him back inside to restock the muffins, because Mr. Cohen had sold nearly everything and the PTA table was his mother's one project this year and she wanted it to go well, wanted people to say the bake sale was the best one.

Jade took out her phone and called her grandmother. It rang twice.

"Did you look it up?" her grandmother said.

"Three months," Jade said. "Faster than any other amendment. And you couldn't vote at eighteen."

A pause, and then the dry laugh Jade had known her whole life. "Well," her grandmother said. "Now you know what you're carrying in your hand. Tell me what the line was like."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
Christian mopped the exam room on Saturday morning while the drip of the anesthesia machine counted time behind him. Monday was the rewrite deadline for his science fair entry, the one the regional committee had rejected with a form letter that praised his "enthusiasm," and his whole project stood on one thing he still could not hold in his head: the path a molecule of glucose took, step by step, until it became the ATP that let a cell keep working. He had taped a diagram above his desk at home, glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then the Krebs cycle turning in the mitochondria like a waterwheel, and every night the wheel slipped loose from its axle again.

At the clinic he had an advantage his bedroom did not have. Mr. Greco let him watch procedures on slow mornings, and the mitochondria were right there, in every animal on the table, doing quietly what Christian was failing to describe on paper. The smell of it all was specific: antiseptic, wet dog, the sweetness of the gas. Today there was a greyhound named Lucy with a racing heart and a liver the size of a football, and there was Anissa, who had volunteered at the clinic since spring and who had also entered the fair, and whose entry, a study of enzyme activity in differently aged dogs, had been accepted.

"You're mopping the same square twice," she said from the doorway, holding a clipboard against her hip.

"I'm thinking."

"About glucose." She said it the way people say the name of a disease. She had seen his diagram, folded into his backpack, the crease running through the whole cycle like a fault line.

In the kennel room the dogs shifted on their blankets when he passed. He crouched by Lucy's run and thought about the heat she gave off, heat that was, his textbook insisted, waste, energy leaked out of the transfers, and he tried to parametrize it in his head, to assign each step a number like a rung on a ladder, glucose in at the top, thirty or so ATP at the bottom, warmth rising off the rungs in between. The numbers would not sit still.

Anissa found him there at noon with two sandwiches from the deli and bad news delivered with judicious slowness. "The committee moved the rewrite deadline," she said. "It's tomorrow, Sunday, five p.m. Not Monday. They emailed this morning." She watched his face. "I'm sorry. I argued with Mrs. Tran about it and she called me a populist for wanting exceptions, which, I looked it up, made even less sense the second time."

That afternoon, between sterilizing instruments and walking a beagle whose owner never came, Christian sat in the waiting room with his phone and searched the name printed in the center of his diagram, the man the cycle was named for. He expected a clean story: genius, discovery, laurels. The screen gave him something crooked. The journal Nature had rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle. Rejected it. Krebs had published in a journal called Enzymologia instead. Christian read the line twice, then held the phone out to Anissa, who was restocking the vaccine fridge.

"Nature turned him down," he said. "The whole cycle. He had to publish it somewhere else."

She took the phone, read, and handed it back. "So the most important thing about how a dog's liver works almost didn't get printed." She looked toward the treatment room, where Lucy slept under a warmed towel, her ribs rising and falling, mitochondria by the billion spending glucose to keep the ribs going.

Christian stayed past his shift. Mr. Greco was monitoring Lucy's heart rate when Christian knocked on the frame of the door, and after a look at the monitor that lasted a long second, the vet waved him in. Christian didn't ask for help. He asked if he could watch, and while he watched he took out his diagram and a pen, and he wrote in the margin, in small letters, "Nature, 1937, no. Enzymologia, yes," because he wanted the fact where he could see it while he worked. Then he walked the ladder again, glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, the fragments carried into the mitochondria, the cycle turning, ATP coming off like sparks off a grinder, and for the first time the order of it felt less like something he had memorized and more like something that had happened in front of him, in Lucy, all afternoon.

He wrote the rewrite that night at the clinic's front desk, the waiting room lights off except the one above the reception computer. He kept what his original entry had gotten wrong, described the correction, and made the Krebs rejection his opening, though he knew the judges might find it cheeky. At five the next afternoon he submitted it with eleven minutes to spare, and on Monday the committee's reply was brief: accepted, no award, revise again before the state round.

When he came in that week, Lucy's run was empty. Anissa was washing her blanket in the utility sink, and she didn't turn around when he stopped in the doorway. "She went home this morning," Mr. Greco called from the back. "Old owner finally answered the phone."

Christian stood there holding his accepted entry form, and Anissa wrung out the blanket and hung it over the rail to dry.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
Grandfather's kitchen smelled of coffee and the vinegar he used on the windows, and Anna spread her chemistry notes across the table where three generations of him had eaten breakfast. The exam was Monday. She had failed the last one, a 61 that had seemed to metastasize through her whole transcript the moment she saw it, and Ms. Holloway had written "come see me" in red at the top, which was almost worse than the grade.

The unit was equilibrium. She understood the arithmetic well enough, the ratios, the constant, but Le Chatelier's principle kept sliding away from her whenever she tried to hold it. A system at equilibrium, disturbed, shifts to oppose the disturbance. She'd copied it onto an index card and read it eleven times on the bus out here, and it still felt like a sentence about people rather than about molecules.

Her grandmother was in the garden pulling the last carrots, impervious to the November wind that had driven Anna inside. Anna carried her notes to the doorway and read aloud, hoping that hearing it would do what reading hadn't. "If you change the temperature, the equilibrium shifts."

"Like the proofing on bread," her grandmother said without straightening up. "Too cold, the yeast sits there and does nothing. You put it near the stove and it wakes up." She snapped a carrot free and held it out. Anna took it and stood there, and something about the warm bowl by the stove, the dough rising too fast and then collapsing when her grandmother moved it, made the principle feel briefly solid. Systems pushed back. They did not like being pushed.

Inside again, she opened the textbook to the practice problems and found the one about ammonia. Nitrogen and hydrogen made ammonia, and the reaction was exothermic, gave off heat, which meant, by the principle, that low temperatures favoured more ammonia at equilibrium. She wrote that out carefully, feeling the satisfaction of a rule applied. Then she turned the page and there was a photograph of an industrial plant, tall silver towers against a grey sky, and a caption that stopped her: the plants ran hot, several hundred degrees, deliberately.

She texted Carley, who was also studying, and then Crosby, who was not. Carley wrote back in fragments: why would a factory choose a temperature that gives less product??? that's so dumb. Anna stared at the caption. It wasn't dumb, or if it was, it was the kind of dumb that cost millions of dollars, which meant it probably wasn't dumb. She sat with the contradiction, pencil tapping, and felt the familiar frustration of a rule that worked until you pointed it at the actual world.

Her grandfather came in from the barn, stamped his boots, and sat down across from her with his coffee. He asked what she was scowling at, and she explained it, the principle, the ammonia, the plant running hotter than the equilibrium wanted. He didn't say anything for a while, which was how he listened. Then he said, "Your great-grandfather ran this place, then my brother was supposed to, then me. The old way. First son." He turned the cup slowly in its saucer. "Everybody thought the rule was the rule. Then my brother went to war and the rule didn't know what to do about that, so we did something else. Rules are for when nothing's happening."

Anna looked down at the photograph. Nothing happening. She thought of her grandmother's dough sitting cold, the yeast inert, technically perfect and completely useless. The cold reaction vessel would hold more ammonia at equilibrium, that was true, that was the rule, and it would also take so long to get there that the truth of it didn't matter. The plant ran hot because cold was too slow. Both things were real at once, and the choice between them wasn't in the chemistry; it was in what you were willing to give up. She wrote "hotter = less ammonia at equilibrium but faster" and underlined it twice, then added a question mark in the margin, because she still couldn't say exactly where the balance fell, what the right temperature was, whether there even was one.

That night she set her notes by the window and texted Carley a summary, then lay in her mother's old bed under the slanted ceiling, listening to the wind work at the shingles. In the morning she would tell Ms. Holloway she understood it, and it would be almost true. Downstairs, her grandmother slid the dough into the oven, having found the warm place and the right time, and closed the door gently, as if the bread might be persuaded.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
Alyssa's grandmother had arrived on Tuesday with a suitcase, a blood pressure cuff, and the announcement that Dr. Okafor had put her on "a plan," which she pronounced the way other people said "prison sentence." On Thursday, Ms. Ngo had assigned the health class exactly this: learn to take and interpret a reading, then explain how diet and exercise could change it. Alyssa took this as fate arranging itself politely for once, and carried the cuff box to the kitchen table like a trophy.

"Sit still," she told her grandmother, who was narrating the entire procedure as though commentating a tennis match. The cuff hissed, the numbers climbed, and Alyssa wrote them down: 148 over 92. She squinted at the little laminated card in the box. The top number, it said, was the pressure when the heart pushed; the bottom, between beats. Below 120 over 80 was where you wanted to live. Her grandmother lived elsewhere, evidently, in a roomier neighborhood.

"That's high," Alyssa said.

"It's Tuesday," her grandmother said, as if that were a unit of measurement.

Alyssa's nascent career as a family health analyst deepened at the pantry. Ms. Ngo had mentioned in passing, one sentence and no more, that the World Health Organization recommended adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which was less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure. Alyssa had written it in her notebook because it sounded like the kind of thing that would later be on a quiz, or, apparently, in her own kitchen. She turned over a can of soup. One can: over 900 milligrams of sodium, nearly half the entire day's allowance, and her grandmother ate soup the way other people drank coffee.

At dinner her grandmother salted the rice before tasting it, which Alyssa considered a hostile act. "Did you know," she began, in the tone she'd learned from her mother, "that a whole day is supposed to be under 2 grams of sodium? And that's less than 5 grams of salt. Your soup alone is almost half."

"I survived a war," her grandmother said, "and I will survive a soup."

Vivian, when Alyssa texted her about it, replied with a photo of her own family's kitchen, three different kinds of seasoned salt visible on the counter, and the message: "we are all going to float away like salted slugs. also did u figure out the exercise part of the assignment or are we just going to be the sodium police." Alyssa laughed into her elbow. The exercise part she had from Ms. Ngo's handout, and from her grandmother's own doctor, who had prescribed walking. Alyssa had a memory of her grandmother, years ago, walking everywhere, before the knee, before the chair by the window became headquarters.

The interesting thing, Alyssa thought while washing dishes, was that the assignment asked for an explanation, not a lecture, and she didn't want to be a tiny health ideologue, cornering her grandmother with a pamphlet. Her grandmother was an adult, enfranchised in every sense, free to salt her rice into next week. But she also wanted to keep her, that was the whole truth of it, and wanting to keep someone and wanting to control them sat side by side on the counter like the salt and the pepper, and Alyssa couldn't always tell which was which.

So on Saturday she tried a different experiment, which was to walk. "The doctor said walking," she announced. "I'm going. Come if you want." She said it to the window, not to her grandmother, and put on her shoes like someone with no stake in the answer. Her grandmother said nothing for a full minute, which for her was a paragraph, and then went to find different shoes. They walked to the pharmacy and back, slowly, her grandmother pointing out which houses used to be bakeries. At the pharmacy Alyssa took her grandmother's pressure at the machine by the film counter, mostly as a joke, and got 144 over 89, which was lower, or which was Thursday, or which was nothing at all yet. One reading proved nothing. Two proved nothing. She was honest enough with herself to know that.

Nevaeh sent her a letter, an actual paper letter, because she was like that, folded into a paper crane that Alyssa had to undo carefully. "Dear salt detective," it read. "For the assignment I said the heart is a pump and the arteries are pipes and sodium is the annoying roommate who makes the pipes retain everything, and Ms. Ngo wrote 'creative, cite your numbers' in red pen, so do your citations better than me. Also my dad's reading was so high the cuff made a sad noise. P.S. if your grandmother starts walking, mine might copy her, they compete about everything."

Monday after school, Alyssa found her grandmother in the kitchen with her reading glasses on, holding the soup can at arm's length like a suspicious letter. "Nine hundred milligrams," her grandmother said. "In a can."

"That's almost half your whole day," Alyssa said. "Under 2 grams for the day, that's the whole target. Less than 5 grams of salt."

Her grandmother set the can down, picked up a different one, and turned it over.

"Do we have the low-sodium kind?" she asked. "Or do I have to learn to like lentils?"

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: If air resistance is ignored, a projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight, because no horizontal force acts on it.
story:
The ledge at the far side of the skate park dropped maybe a meter and a half, and Dario had been launching off it all afternoon, tucking his board under him in the air and landing on the downslope where the concrete curved up again. Daniel sat on the flat bottom of the bowl with a physics worksheet on his knee, a pencil, and a phone calculator he didn't trust. The worksheet said: a ball leaves a ledge at four meters per second, the ledge is 1.5 meters high, how far does the ball travel before hitting the ground. There was a second part about a cliff and a stone, and a third part he hadn't read yet, and all of it was due Monday.

He had failed the last quiz. Not badly, but in a way that felt structural, like a house with one wall missing. His father had responded by attaching conditions to the weekly disbursement of his allowance: a signed note from Ms. Gagnon confirming he'd been to the Tuesday help session, and evidence of actual studying, which his father defined vaguely and enforced literally. Daniel had the note. He had the worksheet. What he didn't have was any idea how to start.

Haylee arrived at four with her own board and a slushie, saw the worksheet, and sat down beside him without being asked. "That's the one Gagnon gave us," she said. "The separation thing."

"I don't know what that means."

"You split it. Up and down is one problem, sideways is another." She pulled the straw out of her slushie and pointed it at Dario, who was pushing back up the slope for another run. "Watch him instead. Seriously. He leaves the ledge at some speed, and the whole time he's in the air, nothing is pushing him sideways. His horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight."

"That's not how it works. He's going to slow down."

"In the air? What's slowing him down?"

Daniel thought about it. On the ground, friction, the roughness of the concrete, his own leg deciding to stop pushing. In the air, none of that was there. "Nothing, I guess. If you ignore air."

"If you ignore air," Haylee agreed, and drank her slushie.

Dario took the run. He crouched at the lip, popped off, hung for a moment that looked longer than it could possibly have been, and came down on the slope with a crack that made two little kids at the rail look over. Daniel wrote down the time on his phone. Then he wrote it again, because the first version of his handwriting was useless, and transcribed the whole messy column of figures into the back of his notebook where the pages were still clean.

"Eight-tenths of a second," he said. "Roughly. I counted three times."

"You counted a skater with your phone," Haylee said. "Gagnon would want you to time something smaller."

"She wants anything. She said come with a question I actually tried to answer." He drew the ledge, the drop, the curve of the downslope, and then, next to it, a clean horizontal line with an arrow. The arrow was Dario's sideways motion, and beside it he wrote the number Haylee had estimated for Dario's speed off the lip, which was a guess dressed up as data, and underneath it he wrote the falling part, which was just the meter and a half of drop. Two problems. One line going across, one line going down.

He did the falling part first, because it was the one with a formula he half remembered. Then the sideways part, which turned out to need almost nothing: the speed, the time, multiplication. The answer said Dario should have crossed about two and a half meters of air before coming down. Daniel paced it off along the bottom of the bowl, heel to toe, and got two and a half meters, give or take a shoe.

"Say that again," Dario said, rolling up to them with his board under one arm. He had the flat, petulant look he got when he suspected people were talking about him. He was seventeen and hated being a data point.

"Your horizontal velocity is constant the whole flight," Daniel said. "That's the whole trick. You go off the ledge at whatever speed, and you keep that exact sideways speed until you land. The fall and the forward don't mix. You solve them separately."

"So I could go farther."

"You could go faster."

Dario looked at the ledge for a while. Then he dropped his board and started pushing toward the far ramp again, faster this time, taking the long diagonal line that the older skaters used. Haylee wrote her name in the margin of Daniel's worksheet next to a correction in the third line of his algebra, where he had dropped a negative sign and then, two lines later, quietly picked it back up without acknowledging it.

"He's going to case it," she said.

He didn't case it. He came off the lip with more speed than the run before, cleared the flat section he'd been landing on, and came down farther along the curve than Daniel's paced-off mark by what looked, to both of them counting from the bottom of the bowl, like most of a meter. Daniel stood where he was. The extra distance could have come from the faster takeoff, which was what his numbers said should happen, or from the way Dario had leaned forward in the air, pumping the board the way they all did without thinking about it, which his numbers said nothing about at all. There was no way, sitting on concrete with a phone and a pencil, to tell which part was which. He wrote both explanations in the margin, one after the other, and did not cross either one out.

Ms. Gagnon was still in the parking lot when they left, loading cones into the trunk of her car. She taught two blocks from the park and came here on Saturdays to watch, though she claimed it was for the coffee place on the corner. Daniel held up the worksheet with the paced-off measurement and the two margin notes and the clean copy of the work, and asked her which one of the two it was.

She looked at the page for longer than the page probably deserved. "Bring that Tuesday," she said. "Both margins. That's the question worth asking."

Dario, already halfway down the sidewalk, called back over his shoulder, "Tell her I'm the constant one."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a stand of pines and came out on a gravel loop above the creek, and Colton had chosen it because the bio test was on Monday and his bedroom had stopped working as a place to think. He carried Mr. Henry's study sheet folded into quarters in his back pocket, soft at the creases from a week of handling. Shiloh and Vienna had come along because Shiloh claimed she studied better while walking and Vienna claimed Shiloh would get lost, and both of them had the same test.

They stopped at the second bench, where the creek ran shallow over flat stones, and spread the notes across the slats. Colton read the first question aloud. Explain how DNA is copied and how a gene becomes a protein. He was supposed to be able to answer it in a paragraph, and so far he could answer it in two sentences that both said the same thing.

"Okay," said Vienna, tapping the page. "Copying. Replication. When a cell divides, it copies its DNA first." She paused. "So the new cell gets all new DNA, right? That's the whole point of copying."

Shiloh shook her head immediately. "No. If it were all new, you'd lose the old one. Nothing gets thrown away in a cell. It's half and half." She held up her hands and began to gesticulate, drawing two invisible ropes and then splitting them apart. "One old piece, one new piece, in each copy."

"That's not what copied means," said Vienna. "When you copy a key, the copy is new. The old key doesn't get split down the middle."

They looked at Colton. He was the one with the sheet, the one who had read the chapter twice, and he understood that looking back at them without an answer would settle the argument worse than anything he could say wrong. He also understood, with a small melancholic clarity, that he did not have the answer. He had read the word. He could almost see it, white on the page, and he could not produce it.

He unfolded the sheet further, flattening it against his knee, and ran his finger down the margin where Mr. Henry had printed vocabulary terms in a column. Semiconservative. He said it out loud, then said it again more slowly, and the shape of the word opened. Semi. Conservative. Keeping half.

"It's called semiconservative," he said. "Each new double helix keeps one strand from the original and pairs it with one newly built strand." He drew it in the gravel with a stick, two lines, then the two lines splitting, each old line getting a new partner beside it. "So you're both kind of right, Vienna. Shiloh's right about the halves. But nothing is lost. Every copy is half the original, and after another copying, those old strands are still out there, each one in a different molecule." He looked at the two diagrams he had scratched into the gravel, side by side, and thought of the original strand still traveling through all the generations of cells, thinning out in the crowd but never gone. He did not say that part out loud.

Vienna leaned over the gravel. "Then why did you freeze just now?"

"Because I'd memorized the word without the picture," he said. "I could define it on a quiz and not know what I was saying." That admission felt like a reparation he owed them, small but real, since he had spent a week acting like the one who knew.

They walked on, and Shiloh, who could not leave a subject until she had squeezed it dry, brought up the second half of the question. How does the gene become a protein. Colton had a paragraph for this one and he delivered it while stepping over a root, hands in his pockets now, the stick abandoned. The gene gets copied into a message, a single-stranded copy that carries the sequence out of the nucleus, and that message gets read in threes, each three-letter group matched to one amino acid, and the amino acids get linked in order, and the chain folds, and the folded chain is the protein.

"So there are two copies," said Vienna. "The semiconservative one that stays, and the message one that goes."

"Right," said Colton, and then he stopped, because he had said it with more certainty than he owned. The message copy was not semiconservative, he was fairly sure, it was just a single strand made off the one template and it didn't hang around, it got broken down after. Fairly sure. He had a memory of a diagram with a dotted line meaning temporary, and he could not confirm the dotted line's meaning from memory. "Actually, don't quote me on the second copy. The semiconservative part I can draw for you. The rest is a paragraph I can recite, and I don't fully know yet where the reciting stops and the knowing starts."

"You're going to write that on the test?" said Shiloh.

"I'm going to draw both things. Tonight. Until I can do it from nothing." He picked up the study sheet, which had gone damp at the edges from the bench, and folded it along its soft creases.

They came out of the pines onto the gravel loop, and the creek was below them again, running fast where the bank narrowed. Vienna asked Mr. Henry's review session was Tuesday or Thursday, and Shiloh said Tuesday, and then neither of them said anything for a stretch, the three of them walking at the pace the trail set. Colton kept turning the picture over, the two lines splitting, the old strand going forward inside every copy, half of every helix a survivor of the original. Somewhere in the middle of that, he took the stick out of his jacket pocket where he had apparently put it without noticing, and threw it sidearm into the creek.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, such as late payments, can be reported for seven years, and bankruptcies for up to ten.
story:
The letter arrived on a Tuesday, addressed to Amy's brother, and because he was at work and the envelope had a window in it, their mother set it on the kitchen table under the fruit bowl, where it sat all afternoon like a second, smaller piece of fruit nobody wanted.

"He's not going to open it," Amy said at dinner. "You know that."

Her mother shrugged, which was answer enough. Amy's brother was nineteen, two years out of high school, and treated mail the way he treated parking tickets, as weather that would eventually pass. Amy took the letter upstairs after the dishes and left it outside his door, and in the morning it was still there, unopened, so she brought it back down and slit it with a paring knife, telling herself she was protecting the table from her mother's simmering.

It was from a credit card company. A payment had been missed in March. There was a number to call and a small box of print, and the print said that late payments could be reported for seven years.

Seven years. She did the math before she could stop herself. He would be twenty-six. Done with whatever school he might still talk himself into, maybe applying for an apartment, maybe a car loan, and March of this year would still be sitting on a file somewhere with his name on it, patient as a stain.

She texted Ria, who knew everything about this because Ria's mother worked at a bank. Ria wrote back fast: seven years for most bad stuff like late payments, ten if it's a bankruptcy. Then: is he bankrupt?? Amy typed no, just one missed payment. Ria sent a single wide-eyed emoji.

Amy called her brother at the tire shop where he worked. "Just call them," she said. "It's one payment."

"It's one payment," he said back, in the voice he used when he thought he was quoting her to expose how dramatic she was. "They'll get over it."

"It's not them getting over it. It's a report. It stays on you for seven years. Seven. And if it were a bankruptcy it'd be ten."

There was a pause long enough that she could hear the shop's air compressor cycling behind him. "Where'd you read that?"

"The letter. And Ria."

"Ria's sixteen."

"So is the letter." She gripped the phone. "You're going to be you for a lot longer than you're planning for."

He laughed, but it came out thin, and he said he'd call them on break, and then he didn't say anything else, and neither did she.

She walked the long way to Mr. Henry's house that afternoon to return the casserole dish her mother had sent over with her, because walking helped her think and because Mr. Henry always let her think out loud without ever picking a side. He was in the garage sanding a drawer, and she told him the whole thing, the letter, the seven years, the ten, her brother's voice on the phone.

Mr. Henry kept sanding. "When I was his age," he said finally, "I thought being young was a costume I could take off. Clean slate every morning." He blew dust off the wood. "Turns out the slate keeps everything. You just learn which marks you can live with."

"That's not comforting."

"Wasn't trying to be."

She sat on an upturned bucket and watched his hands. She'd been arguing with her brother like time was a trick being played on him, but that wasn't quite her real position, and she didn't want to hold a position she didn't believe just because it won the argument. The truth was messier: she thought he was wrong to shrug, and she also thought that a person shouldn't have to be perfect at nineteen, and she could not find any clean line where mercy stopped and accountability started. Chemistry was easier that way; carbon was carbon, but graphite and diamond were allotropes of it, the same element arranged differently, and the arrangement decided everything. People kept rearranging themselves, and the file kept the old arrangement anyway.

"Mr. Henry," she said. "Did you ever have something follow you?"

The sanding stopped.

"Seven years," he said. "Or ten?"

"I don't know yet."

He set the drawer down and looked at it, not at her, for a long moment, and Amy realized she had no idea which of them he was answering.

"Would you tell me if it was on yours?" she asked.

He picked up the sandpaper again. "Go home before your mother sends out a search party."

She carried the casserole dish back up the street with both hands, and it was only halfway home that she understood he'd never actually said no.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
The line outside the fire hall was longer than Anais had expected, folding itself twice around the parking lot the way it did in the photographs her civics teacher used to show, and she stood in it holding the sample ballot her mother had circled in blue pen. Somewhere behind her, Brady was telling Jayla about the research he'd stayed up doing.

"So Australia," he said, "has had compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925. You have to show up. If you don't vote and you don't have a valid reason, you get fined. Actual money."

"You're making that up," Jayla said.

"Look it up. I did, twice, because I didn't believe it either."

Anais turned around. "Fined how much?"

"Enough that you'd notice. I didn't get the exact number, but skipping isn't free there, that's the whole point."

The line moved, and she moved with it, chewing on this. In her house voting was treated like weather, something you did not get to opt out of, and her father had a way of saying not voting is voting that she'd found smug for most of her life. But Brady's fact had destabilized something in her anyway, because a fine meant the government thought a citizen's absence was worth money, the way the city thought parking illegally was worth money, and she couldn't decide whether that made voting more sacred or less. She held both ideas and could not get them to lie flat against each other.

Jayla was quiet, hugging her jacket. "My mom's working doubles all week," she said finally. "She's not coming. She said one vote, whatever."

"Do you think she should get fined?" Brady asked it lightly, but Anais heard the weight under it.

"No," Jayla said. "I think she should get a break."

Inside the hall, the noise dropped to the squeak of shoes and the paper shuffle, and a woman with a clipboard whose name tag said Ms. Adebayo found Anais's street on her list and walked her to the right table without being asked, slowing down when Anais hesitated at the partition between the lettered rows. "First time?" Ms. Adebayo said, and when Anais nodded, she didn't say congratulations or anything with gravitas; she just tapped the booth's edge. "Take as long as you want. There's no prize for finishing first."

The ballot had more on it than the sample had. A county question she hadn't studied, about protected land along the creek, a riparian corridor, the words said, some wording about setbacks and buffers that she read twice and understood about two thirds of. She thought of the creek behind Jayla's building, the heron that stood in it in the mornings like it was being paid to. She thought of her mother's blue circles, which stopped at the first page.

She filled in the ovals she was sure about, then the ones she was reasonably sure about, and then sat with the county question while the machine at the front beeped for somebody else's ballot, once, twice. Compulsory or not, she was here, and being here meant deciding things she hadn't earned the right, yet, to feel confident about. That was the part nobody had warned her of. The fine in Australia got you in the door; it didn't tell you what to do once you were standing in the booth.

She marked yes on the creek, on the theory that the heron had been there longer than the county had, and fed the sheet through the machine and watched it vanish with a sound like a held breath released.

Outside, Jayla and Brady were waiting on the curb, and the afternoon had gone gold the way it did in October, early and brief. "I voted on the creek thing," Anais said. "I'm still not sure it was right."

"That's allowed," Brady said.

"I know it's allowed." But she was glad he'd said it anyway. She took out her phone and texted her mother two words, then put it away before the reply came, because Jayla was holding out a hand for a piece of the licorice she'd been guarding all afternoon, and Anais broke off the longer half.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing.
story:
Hunter spread the two leases across the hood of his mother's car, one from the Riverside complex and one from a duplex on Colfax, and weighted their corners with socket wrenches so the garage draft from under the door wouldn't shuffle them. The overhead bulb swung a little whenever the wind found the gap, and the pages moved in and out of shadow like they were breathing. His mother had put them on the kitchen counter that morning before her night shift, next to a note that said only, Which one. She hadn't said what would happen if the answer was neither.

He had a calculator app open on his phone and his last three pay stubs from the grocery store, where he stocked shelves four nights a week. Riverside wanted nine hundred and eighty a month plus a flat seventy-five for water and trash, with electricity paid by the tenant. The Colfax duplex was eight ninety with all utilities included except internet, but it wanted first and last month up front plus a deposit, and Hunter had already done that sum twice and it came to more than they had in the account both times.

Weston came through the side door without knocking, the way he always did, carrying two cans of soda and the phlegmatic calm he carried into everything, including the time his own family had moved twice in one year. He set a can on the Riverside lease, leaving a ring Hunter would have to explain later.

"You're doing homework in the garage now?"

"It's not homework." Hunter pulled the Colfax page out from under the soda ring. "It's real. My mom wants me to figure out which one we can afford, and I don't know how to compare them, because one has utilities bundled in and one doesn't, and the electric bill changes with the season."

"So call the electric company."

"I did. The woman gave me an average for a two-bedroom in that zip code, but she said winter is higher, and I don't know if she was giving me a January number or a spread-over-the-year number. She was rushing. It sounded like a January number."

Malia arrived twenty minutes later with a folder of debate materials, because she had regionals on Saturday and had been rehearsing her elocution in the driveway until Hunter texted her that the garage had better acoustics anyway. She stood over the hood of the car and read both leases top to bottom without touching them, which Hunter appreciated, because he was beginning to think of the pages as evidence.

"Okay," she said. "So operationalize it. Turn 'can we afford it' into a number, or you'll just be arguing vibes with your mom at seven in the morning."

Hunter thought about that. He wrote his monthly take-home pay at the top of a clean sheet: eleven hundred and forty dollars, if he kept his current hours. His mother's income was the harder thing, tips and shifts that moved around, so he used the lowest month from her bank statements he could bring himself to look at. Then he added the electric estimate to Riverside, divided the total by their combined income, and got a decimal he had to convert twice because he didn't believe it the first time. Thirty-four percent. He did Colfax the same way, utilities already inside the rent, and got thirty-one.

"That seems high," Weston said, reading over his shoulder.

Hunter typed into his phone, what percentage of income should go to rent. The answer came back from a government housing page, and he read it twice with his thumb hovering over the screen. "In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing."

"Cost-burdened," Malia repeated, trying the phrase out the way she tried out lines for her speech, testing its weight in her mouth. "That's the word for it."

Hunter sat down on the milk crate by the workbench. Both apartments made them cost-burdened, one by a hair and one by a margin, and the number hadn't been hiding anywhere, it had just been sitting there in the open waiting for him to divide. But the Riverside estimate was built on a phone call with a rushing woman in a call center, and his mother's income was built on a month he'd picked for a reason he couldn't fully defend, and the Colfax deposit would empty them out before they even signed. He didn't know which uncertainty was bigger. He knew only that both answers were over the line, and that the line was real, and that his mother would read the number and decide something anyway.

He copied both percentages onto the back of the Colfax lease in pencil, then wrote under them, Colfax if the winter electric estimate is high. It was the kind of note that said more than it said. Weston cracked the second soda and set it, unopened, on the workbench beside the crate, and Malia gathered her folder and said she'd run her speech for them before she left, since they looked like they needed the distraction. Hunter listened to the first minute of it with the leases still fanned across the hood of the car, the bulb swinging, both percentages waiting for morning.

"The question," Malia was saying, to the lawnmower and the shadowed boxes and the two boys, "is not whether we can pay. The question is what paying costs."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Jesse would tell anyone who asked that he was not nervous about directing his first one-act, and he told people often, twice before breakfast on Monday and once more on the walk to the theatre building at drama camp, which was why Vivian kept count on her fingers behind his back. He had the binder, the clipboard, the three sharpened pencils. He had, most importantly, a system, which was nine pennies and one dime arranged on the picnic table outside the dining hall, each coin standing for one actor in his cast. He was, by his own account, completely fine.

"It's a model stage," he explained to Abigayle, who had come over with her cereal and a suspicion of anything Jesse described as a system. "The table is the floor. The pennies are the actors. The dime is Ricky, because he's taller."

"That's not how height works," Abigayle said, but she moved a penny anyway, sliding it downstage, and something in Jesse's chest went quiet and organized. The play was about two sisters dividing their dead mother's kitchen, which was heavy material for a Thursday afternoon at a camp better known for its talent show skits about sentient cafeterias, and Jesse had chosen it partly for that heaviness, though he'd have said he chose it for the craft. He had wanted, if he was honest with himself in the small hours, to be taken seriously. He was not going to be honest in the small hours. He was going to arrange pennies.

Rehearsal one was a disaster he would later describe as "a productive start." The actors stood where they pleased, which meant clustered upstage like nervous cattle, and when Jesse asked them to move they drifted back within minutes, as if the back wall exerted some gentle parasitism, feeding on their nerve. Ricky delivered his big monologue to the lighting booth. Jesse, whose directions had been confident in the dorm and laconic in practice, found that his voice came out in the register of a person apologizing for existing.

That night he found Vivian in the lounge and told her the whole thing had gone fine, actually, really well, just some early kinks. Vivian said, "You texted me 'everything is on fire' at four o'clock." Jesse said that was a metaphor for kinks. She looked at him the way you look at a coin you suspect is foreign currency.

It was Mr. Tanaka who left the theatre history book on the prop shelf, or at least the book was there when Jesse went hunting for a better table to build his model on, and nobody else used the prop shelf, so the attribution seemed safe. He sat on the floor with it, expecting to skim. Instead he stopped at a picture of a miniature stage with little wooden figures, tiny and grave, frozen mid-scene. Nineteenth-century directors had planned their scenes on model stages, the caption said, and W. S. Gilbert, of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas, had used a block for each actor. That was where the word came from. Blocking. Not blocking someone's way, not blocking a shot, but little blocks on a little stage, moved around by a person pacing a room alone, deciding where everyone should stand.

"Oh," Jesse said, out loud, to the prop shelf.

The next morning he brought the book to the picnic table and set his pennies on the picture, so they could learn from their ancestors. Abigayle arrived, and he showed her, holding up a penny. "This is a block," he said. "The word blocking comes from directors like W. S. Gilbert, planning scenes on a model stage with a block for each actor."

"So we've been doing nineteenth-century cosplay with pocket change," Abigayle said. "That's the best thing that's happened at this camp."

"It's not cosplay. It's lineage."

"It's a dime standing in for a tall boy, Jesse. It's cosplay."

But here was the thing he didn't say, because he hadn't fully sorted it: the book changed his mind about something he'd been protecting. He had been directing by dictation, moving the actors like the coins, as though people were objects to be slid, and when they slid back he'd taken it as defiance. Gilbert's blocks didn't resist, though. Gilbert's blocks didn't get stage fright or develop opinions about their motivation. The model was a plan, not a performance. Somewhere between the pennies and the people, the actors had to be asked.

Rehearsal two began with Jesse doing something that felt physically dangerous, which was admitting the situation. "I planned you all on a table," he told the cast, holding up the coffee tin of coins. "Here's Marta, here's Dot, here's the actor playing Dot's ex-husband, who will henceforth be a nickel." There was laughter, good laughter, the kind with oxygen in it. Then he asked them, before placing anyone, where they thought their characters would stand in the kitchen, and Marta said she wanted to be near the sink the whole play because her mother had always been at the sink, and Jesse stood there feeling the penny plan in his head quietly reorganize itself around a person.

He did still use the coins. He laid the tin out on the stage floor during breaks, and the actors gathered around and argued about where the nickel should go, and Ricky, tall as promised, leaned over everyone saying "if I'm the dime I want the dime to face the audience," and Abigayle said the dime had no face, and Ricky said all currency had faces, and this went on for a while in a way that Jesse would later call productive.

What remained unresolved, and Jesse was honest about this with exactly one person, was whether the heaviness was getting through. The blocking was clean now, the sisters split by the invisible kitchen counter, and Mr. Tanaka watched the last run-through from the back with an expression that could have been approval or gas, though Jesse was fairly sure he'd seen a nod, and Vivian claimed she'd definitely seen two nods, and one of them was probably exaggerating, and neither would concede which.

On the night of the performance, before house opened, Jesse took the coffee tin to the lip of the stage and poured the coins out and arranged them one last time, by feel, in the dark, the way he imagined Gilbert pacing his model stage with his little blocks, deciding alone and then letting the people decide too. He heard the audience settling in beyond the curtain, hundreds of them by his estimate, or forty, but definitely hundreds. He set the nickel downstage left and held it there a second, then let it go.

"Places," he said, and shook the tin until it was empty.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
story:
Makayla had the kitchen to herself for exactly two hours, which her mother had established the way treaties are established, with borders and consequences. The thermometer was clipped to the pot. The chocolate was chopped. The marble slab, borrowed from Mr. Ferreira next door, sat on the counter like a small country waiting to be invaded.

"You're hovering," she said into her phone, which was propped against the sugar jar with Marisol on video call.

"I'm mentoring from a distance. That's different."

"You tempered exactly once."

"And mine snapped," Marisol said. "When I broke a piece off it made that sound, like a proper chocolate bar. Yours last time bent. It bent, Makayla. Chocolate should not bend."

Makayla stirred and did not answer, because the answer was yes, it had bent, gray and streaked and soft at the corners, like something that had given up. She had spread it on the slab anyway and scraped and scraped, and it had gone from glossy to dull to a kind of stubborn paste, and she had eaten her failure in small shameful squares while watching a video about couches.

The flashback came uninvited, the way they do. Last spring, Mr. Ferreira had stood in his kitchen in his reading glasses, holding a bar of chocolate up to the window and snapping it in half so cleanly that the sound arrived before she understood what had made it. "My mother did this every December," he had said, and then, as if embarrassed by the reverence, "It's mostly just patience and a thermometer." He had lent her the slab that same afternoon, wrapped in a dish towel, and told her not to drop it on her foot, which she had nearly done twice since.

Now she poured the melted chocolate onto the marble and began working it with the spatula, spreading it thin, gathering it back, spreading again. The smell rose up and she fell into a brief reverie, imagining herself in some future version of this kitchen, someone's competent aunt, snapping bars for nieces. Then the chocolate began to thicken faster than she expected, seizing toward paste, and the reverie collapsed.

"It's doing the thing," she said. "It's doing the thing again."

"Temperature?"

"Too low, I think. I worked it too long." She scraped it back into the pot and stared at it, sitting there lumpy and wrong, and felt the tectonic sort of shift that happens when a plan fails quietly: no shouting, just the ground moving under you.

"Okay, wait," Marisol said. "When mine worked, I didn't even have a slab yet. Remember, I texted you from my grandma's kitchen."

"You used the bar I gave you. The leftover one from Christmas."

"Right, because it was already tempered, from the store. That's the whole trick. You chop it fine and stir it into the melted chocolate, and the melted part copies it." Marisol shrugged on the screen. "Seeding, it's called. My grandma called it cheating, but her scale was broken so her opinion was suspect."

Makayla looked at the pot, then at the counter, where a half bar of decent chocolate sat in its wrapper, left over from something. She unwrapped it and chopped it into small pieces, quick and careless, the knife going tick tick tick against the board.

"If this ruins it, you're buying me chocolate."

"If this ruins it, you ruined it. I'm just the camera."

She waited until the thermometer climbed back up, then stirred the chopped pieces in a handful at a time. They held their shape at first, then softened at the edges, then gave in. She kept stirring, slower now, watching for the shine. There was no way to see the moment it happened, which was the part she disliked most about the whole business, the part she would have to admit she still didn't understand. Something invisible was arranging itself, or it wasn't, and she would only know later, from the evidence.

She dipped a knife tip and swiped a thin stripe onto parchment, and they both watched it in silence, the way you watch a kettle.

"It's setting fast," Marisol said.

"That means something. Good or bad, it means something."

The stripe lost its wet look and went satiny, and when she touched it, it was dry, it was smooth, it looked, if she was honest, like something a shop would charge real money for. The actual test would come when she poured the rest, when it set in the mold, when she turned it out and broke it and listened.

Behind her, the front door opened and closed. Her mother's voice came down the hall, unhurried, carrying a bag of groceries.

"Whatever that smell is," her mother called, "I want some."

Makayla picked up the pot and tipped it toward the mold.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
story:
Daniel had taped the population pyramid to the kitchen window so the light came through the paper, and the bars of it looked almost like something alive. On the left were the males, on the right the females, stacked in five-year age groups from zero to four at the bottom up to eighty-five and older at the top. Ms. Wanjiru had assigned each of them a country and a question: would this place need more schools or more nursing homes? Daniel had drawn the town of Milton Keynes, which had felt like a joke at first, a geography teacher assigning England's most famous new town, until he understood she had chosen it on purpose.

The town's pyramid had a fat bar at the bottom. Wide at zero to four, still wide at five to nine, and then, higher up, the bars narrowed sharply, because the town had been built in the sixties for young families and the young families had stayed young only for a while. He was supposed to present a prediction, and the presentation was tomorrow, and he had nothing but a shape on a window.

He called Casey, who was doing the same assignment for Japan and complaining about it. "Mine's upside down compared to yours," Casey said. "The bottom's skinny and the top's heavy. It's a vase, not a pyramid."

"Mine's a lightbulb," Daniel said. "Fat at the bottom, thin everywhere else."

"Great, so you'll say schools, and I'll say nursing homes, and we'll both get sevens."

He didn't want a seven. He wanted to say something that felt true, and the shape alone didn't feel true yet, because a shape was only one moment, a photograph of a town frozen on a single day. The question underneath the question, the one he kept circling, was whether you could look at a photograph and hear movement in it. His grandfather, who had lived with them since spring and who was impecunious in the way of men who had outlived their savings, drifted through the kitchen for his afternoon tea and paused at the window.

"Graphs," his grandfather said, in the tone of a man greeting an old enemy.

"Population," Daniel said. "The town has all these little kids, and I'm supposed to say what it'll need next."

His grandfather looked at the paper for a long moment, sipped his tea, and said only, "Everything that is young gets older at the same speed," and went to the garden. Daniel stared after him, then back at the pyramid. It was so obvious it embarrassed him. Each bar was five years wide, so every five years, everyone moved up exactly one bar. The fat bar of babies at the bottom would be the fat bar of five-to-nine-year-olds in five years, then the ten-to-fourteen bar after that. The bulge climbed the pyramid like a bead of water up a windowpane. He took a pencil and traced it upward, bar by bar, and wrote beside each one what grade those children would be in: babies now, primary school within five years, and the high school would take the whole bulge roughly ten to fifteen years on.

He texted Casey: "It moves. One bar every five years. It's not a photograph, it's a frame of a film." Casey replied with a row of exclamation marks and then, "Mine moves too but downward, the wide part is at the top and it just gets wider as everyone ages. Nursing homes confirmed." Daniel laughed, then stopped, because he noticed something that unsettled his neat answer. Above the fat bottom bars on his pyramid, there was a second smaller bulge, up in the forty-five to forty-nine range. Two bulges. Two futures. The town would need the schools first, and then, when the fat bead of babies was old and the smaller bead above it was older still, it would need both at once. When he'd asked Ms. Wanjiru in class whether a country could need both, she'd said something about false choices, and he'd thought she was dodging. Now he wasn't sure she had been. Maybe the honest answer was a matter of timing, of which need arrived at which bar, and maybe presenting that honestly was harder and better than picking a side. He also had to admit he couldn't say how big the bars would be after the current ones aged, because children not yet born had no bar at all, and that uncertainty could extenuate his prediction's weakness but not remove it.

He spent the evening making a second sheet, a series of the same pyramid redrawn at intervals, the bulge creeping upward like a slow pulse. His mother asked what he was doing at the table so late, and he tried to explain that a town was not really a shape but a rhythm, that the graph was a kind of physiology, the way a body's needs changed as it grew and aged, and she said, "You sound like your grandfather," which he took as a compliment and which he suspected was not entirely intended as one.

The twist came at ten, when Casey called back, out of breath. "I got it wrong," Casey said. "Japan's top bars are wide because people are living longer, but listen, I found the Milton Keynes census follow-up. The birth rate dropped after the boom. Your bulge doesn't just climb, it thins as it goes." Daniel looked at his traced pencil line, at the neat bead he had drawn climbing the windowpane, and felt the answer shift under him. Thinner as it climbed, but still fatter than the bars around it; still enough children to fill a high school that was built for fewer. He sharpened his pencil and started the redraw again, and his grandfather's teacup sat rinsed and upside down by the sink, waiting for morning.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream, a flow oceanographers call 30 sverdrups.
story:
The planetarium had been booked for the astronomy club, but the projector was broken, so Mr. Nasser dragged in a whiteboard and told them they would do oceanography instead, because climate was climate whether you looked up or down. John sat in the back row with Roxane, who wanted the projector fixed and said so twice before the lights dimmed for nothing. On the whiteboard, Mr. Nasser had taped a printout of the North Atlantic, arrows curled like handwriting across it, and he said that whoever could stand up at the end of the hour and explain why London winters were milder than they had any right to be would get the extra credit. John needed the extra credit. His midterm average was hanging by a thread he could feel every time he opened his grade portal, and his father had already said the word "scholarship" three times that week in the tone people use for a debt.

He leaned forward and copied the map into his notebook, arrows and all, and immediately got them wrong. The loop he drew off Florida bent east too early, and when he compared his page to the printout the difference was small, the kind of thing he would have metabolized as carelessness a year ago and forgotten. He didn't forget it now. He erased it and drew it again, slower, and Roxane watched him do it without comment, which from her was a comment.

"You're drawing it like wind," she said finally. "Wind goes wherever it wants. Water piles up."

"Water goes downhill. There's no downhill in an ocean."

"There's downhill everywhere. It's just flat-looking."

Mr. Nasser overheard none of this, or pretended to. He had put a worksheet on each desk with a single question on it, a number and a unit, and told them nothing else. John read the sheet four times. About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream. Then, in smaller print: oceanographers call this 30 sverdrups. He said the word under his breath and it sounded like a cough, like something Scandinavian, like a name that belonged to a person rather than a quantity.

"Thirty million cubic metres," Roxane said, reading over his arm. "Per second."

"Say it with rivers. How big is a river."

"Big rivers, a few thousand cubic metres a second. Maybe." She frowned. "I don't actually know."

"So this is, what, thousands of rivers." He tried to picture it and couldn't. The number refused to become anything. It sat on the page like a phone number, exact and mute. He raised his hand and asked Mr. Nasser how big a sverdrup was, and Mr. Nasser said, "That's the wrong question," and moved on to the next desk, and John sat there feeling the wrong question burn a hole in him.

The hour thinned out. Half the class had stopped trying, and Nicholas, two rows up, was drawing fish on his worksheet with a highlighter. Roxane had gone quiet in the way that meant she was solving something, and John watched her mouth move around the unit. "Sverdrup," she said. "Sverdrups. It's called sverdrups. Somebody named Sverdrup must have existed, and they named the water after him."

"Thirty of them," John said. "Thirty million cubic metres a second through a strait you could almost see from a plane. And that's the thing, that's not even the interesting part."

"Then what is?"

He looked at the map again, at the arrow leaving Florida and running north and east, and at the little dots marking Norway and Britain sitting at latitudes that matched Labrador, which he knew was frozen most of the year. The same distance from the pole, two completely different worlds. He had always assumed latitude was destiny, the way people assume it, an almost atavistic faith that the sun's angle settled everything, and here was a squiggle of water arguing otherwise. The arrows weren't decoration. They were the explanation, and the explanation was that the ocean moved heat the way a furnace moves heat through pipes, except the pipes were made of the same stuff they carried.

"Wait," he said. "I think I can do this."

"London?"

"London." He stood up before Mr. Nasser could call on anyone else, and his voice came out steadier than he felt. "Warm water leaves the Florida Straits, thirty million cubic metres of it every second, which is thirty sverdrups, and it runs northeast across the Atlantic. It doesn't stay where the sun put it. It carries the warmth somewhere else, and the somewhere else is us. Northern Europe. So London is mild because Florida is hot, basically. Florida's heat gets delivered."

"By courier," Nicholas said, without looking up from his fish.

"By courier that never stops," John said, and sat down, and his heart was going hard, and Mr. Nasser wrote something in his book and said, "Better than most of them," which from Mr. Nasser was a parade.

Roxane caught him at the door afterward, in the dome's half-dark, under the dead projector. "You were wrong about one thing," she said. "You said it carries warmth to us. You said Europe like you live there."

"My dad's applying for a job in London."

She stopped. The subtlety of it landed on her slowly, the extra credit and the map and the moving, all of it one project. "So you're learning to explain their weather."

"I'm learning to explain the weather to a father who thinks I'm failing." He zipped his bag. "There's a version where the current slows down and London gets cold. I read that somewhere. I don't know if it's true or how much or when. I left it out."

"You left out the part you don't know."

"I left out the part I can't defend yet."

She nodded at that, or seemed to, and pushed the door open into the hallway, where the fluorescent light was ordinary and nobody was thinking about the Atlantic. Mr. Nasser was still inside erasing the whiteboard, and through the gap in the door John heard him mutter to himself, "Thirty million a second, and they name it after a Norwegian."

"Actually," John called back, "I looked it up during your class. It's named after the guy who ran the institute, not the guy who found it."

Mr. Nasser lowered the eraser. "Get out of my planetarium."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
story:
The textbook lay open on the picnic table, held flat against the wind by a can of sparkler soda and Sarah-Eve's elbow. Robyn had her knees drawn up on the bench, squinting at a diagram of a DNA strand, and Sarah could tell from the set of her mouth that something was wrong.

"Here," Robyn said, tapping a base in the example problem. "The answer key says the original has an A here, but my copy printed a G. Except the protein at the end is the same. Both versions." She looked up. "So one of them is a typo, or I'm losing my mind."

Sarah leaned over. The mutated strand sat there in black and white, one letter swapped, and the finished protein below it ran the same amino acids either way. She checked twice, tracing the codons with her finger, mouthing the base pairs. "No, you read it right. It's the same protein."

"That can't be how it works. A mutation should do something." Robyn's voice had the thin edge it got when she felt the material turning on her. She'd failed the first quiz, and although she never said so, everyone in Ms. Reyes's class knew it, which was its own quiet cruelty.

"Wait," Sarah said, and pulled the chapter toward her. "Look at the codon table. This one codes for the amino acid, and this one codes for it too. Different letters, same amino acid." She turned the book so Robyn could see, her finger moving between two cells of the table. "So if the mutation lands there, nothing changes."

Robyn stared at it for a long moment. "Then some mutations don't matter at all?"

Sarah ran down the table, matching codons to amino acids, and found it again and again, pairs and even little clusters all pointing to the same building block. "They have a name for these," she said, half remembering a line from the lecture she'd half slept through. "Silent mutations. My dad's a lawyer and even he knew that one. He talks about it whenever he wants to sound smart at dinner, right before he brings up some subpoena he served on a lab." She smiled. "Which is the only genetics he knows."

Sarah-Eve laughed, and Robyn's shoulders came down an inch. She copied the codon table into her notebook, slowly, and Sarah watched her hesitation fade into something steadier. It reminded Sarah of the summer her grandmother, taciturn and stubborn, had tried to teach her to garden in this same backyard, kneeling in the dirt with a trowel, saying almost nothing, correcting only with her hands. When Sarah had planted the tomatoes too close together, her grandmother hadn't explained crowding or roots. She'd just pulled one seedling up, moved it a foot over, and pressed the soil down. It took Sarah years to understand that the lesson was the moving, not the telling. Maybe teaching anything worked like that: you couldn't hand someone the understanding, you could only move the pieces and let them watch.

Robyn lifted her pen. "Okay, so walk me through it. The whole thing, transcription and translation, like I'm five."

"Like you're you," Sarah said. She took a clean sheet and drew the double helix as two wavy lines, then the mRNA peeling off as a single ribbon. "The DNA unzips, and an RNA copy gets made off one strand. That's transcription. Then the copy goes out, the ribosome reads it in threes, and each three-letter word picks an amino acid. That's translation. The amino acids get chained up and that chain folds into the protein."

"And if a letter changes but the word still picks the same amino acid," Robyn said, "the protein comes out identical anyway."

"Right. Silent."

Sarah-Eve, who had been quiet through all of this, rolled a peach across the table toward Robyn without a word, the way she did when she thought someone needed something they hadn't asked for. Robyn took it, and after a moment she took a bite, and then she drew the mutated strand again from memory, the G where the A had been, and beneath it wrote out the amino acids one by one, checking each codon against the table.

She reached the end and set her pen down. "Same protein," she said. "Both of them."

Sarah looked at the two columns, identical, and at the small difference hiding inside them, and understood that she could say she'd mastered this now and still not be sure why the code had been built with so much slack in it, why the cell could shrug off certain wounds. That part she couldn't explain yet. "Quiz me on it tomorrow," she said, "before class."

Robyn closed the notebook and held it against her chest like something she meant to keep. "Deal," she said, and reached over to steal a second bite of the peach.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
story:
The afternoon light through the lab windows turned the cobalt solution a flat, institutional blue, and Savannah leaned over the data table Addison had printed out, running her pencil down the column of numbers. Three temperatures, three values of K. The numbers fell as the temperatures rose, which was the opposite of what she would have guessed, and she had guessed, out loud, in front of Leanne, and been wrong.

"Maybe the table's a mistake," Leanne said, not looking up from her notebook, where she was copying the values in her small, fierce handwriting. It had become a mannerism of hers, this insistence on transcribing everything by hand, as though the printer could not be trusted with facts that mattered.

"It's not a mistake." Addison spun a beaker slowly on the bench. "It's an exothermic reaction. That's the whole point of the exercise. Mr. O'Brien wouldn't hand us a typo on a graded lab."

Savannah thought about her mother, who had wanted her to take the retail job at the garden centre this summer instead of the summer chemistry intensive, and who had said, in the car, that some doors cost more to open than they were worth. She had said it as though it were wisdom. Savannah had not answered, and the silence had sat between them for the whole drive, and she still did not know whether it had been stubbornness or honesty. The intensive had cost her the job, the money, most of her friends' last summer before college. She was here, in any case, in a lab that smelled faintly of sulfur, with two people she had known for four weeks, arguing about a column of numbers.

"So if you heat an exothermic reaction," she said slowly, "the equilibrium constant goes down. And if you cool it, the constant goes up." She turned the pencil over and wrote it in the margin, then looked up. "Then for an endothermic one it has to be the other way around. Raising the temperature raises the constant."

Leanne set her pen down. "How do you know that part? That's not in the table."

"It's not in the table," Savannah admitted. "It's just that they can't both go the same direction, or the word would mean nothing." She hesitated, because she was aware that this was not evidence, it was only a shape she wanted the world to have. "I think it's right. I can't prove it from what we have."

From the doorway, Mr. O'Brien watched them for a moment before he crossed the room. He had a way of arriving at a bench exactly when a mistake was about to become a lesson, and Addison, who had been through two years of his classes, had learned to dread it. He did not correct anything. He set down a second data table, for an endothermic system, said only "for comparison," and walked on to the next group.

Addison found the column first. At the higher temperature, the values of K were larger, not smaller. She checked it twice, because she did not want to be the one who announced something false, and because she was beginning to realize that Savannah, whom she had privately liked since the second day of the intensive, was the kind of person who wanted to be right more than she wanted to be liked, and Addison had not yet decided what she felt about that. She slid the sheet across the bench without a word, letting the numbers do the talking, the way you hand someone a photograph you don't want to caption.

Savannah read it, and Addison watched her face do something complicated, pride and discomfort arriving at the same time. Savannah had guessed the direction correctly, but she had also, Addison knew, implied that Leanne's caution was timidity, and Leanne had gone quiet in the particular way that meant she had registered it and filed it away.

"It's the same principle," Savannah said to Leanne, carefully. "The exothermic one falls when you heat it, and this one rises. I shouldn't have said it like I was sure before the table came."

Leanne shrugged, a small movement that could have meant anything. "You were sure. That's not a crime."

They finished the analysis in a quieter register, Savannah writing the conclusion while Leanne checked each line and Addison washed the glassware nobody had asked her to wash. The lab emptied around them in stages. At the last bench, drying her hands, Addison thought about how she had once quit the debate team rather than tell a partner she thought her argument was hollow, and how that had felt like kindness at the time and felt, now, in this light, more like an inability to be useful. She wasn't sure which it had been. She put the beaker back on the rack.

Mr. O'Brien collected their sheets at the door, read the conclusion standing up, and looked at Savannah over the paper. "You hedged the endothermic claim," he said. "Why?"

"Because I only had it by symmetry, not by evidence," Savannah said. "I'd rather be honest about what I don't know than pretend the table said something it didn't."

He marked something in red at the top of the page, handed it back, and moved on to the next group without telling her whether that had been the right answer.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
Austin had forty-one dollars in his checking account and a guitar amp sitting in the pawnshop window on Miller Street, tagged at two hundred and thirty. The tag had been there for two weeks. Every afternoon on his walk home from school he checked whether the price had dropped, and every afternoon it hadn't, and every afternoon somebody different came out of the pawnshop looking either pleased or gouged.

The credit union was next door, which was how the whole thing started. He'd gone in to cash the birthday check from his grandmother, twenty-five dollars, and while he waited he read the brochure rack, because the line was long and the posters were worse. One brochure showed a tortoise with a stack of coins. Another said something about building credit early. The tortoise, he decided, was meant to be encouraging.

"Are you a member?" the teller asked when he finally reached the window. She said it the way people say hello.

"I have an account. My mom opened it."

"You can open your own now, at seventeen. With a parent on it." She slid the check back with the cash. "There's a student card, too, if you're interested. Low limit."

That night at dinner he brought it up, and his mother said the word "credit card" in the tone she usually reserved for the neighbor's dog. Her own history with cards was a drawer in the kitchen full of statements she called her twenties. She didn't tell him not to get one. She told him what could happen if he got one, which was a different thing, and he mostly heard the sound of her voice rather than the content.

At school the next day he found Gabryel in the library, copying Spanish homework with the grim efficiency of someone who had done the reading and resented it. Gabryel's family ran a shop, and Gabryel understood money in a way that never showed up in math class.
