"So don't carry a balance," Gabryel said, when Austin laid it out. "My dad says the card companies bank on you paying the minimum. That's where they get you. The interest."

"Interest," Austin said, to hear it out loud.

"You borrow two hundred, you end up paying more than two hundred. Over time. That's the whole business model." Gabryel turned a page. "Meanwhile savings go the other way, if you have any, which I don't, because my allowance is a myth."

Austin took the brochure to Ms. Walker after sixth period, because she was the one teacher who answered questions honestly instead of aspirationally. She looked at the fine print, then handed it back without a speech, which he appreciated.

"What does grace period mean?" he asked. "It's in here three times and it doesn't say."

"That's for you to read closely," she said. "But ask me again if the pamphlet stonewalls you."

He read it that night, twice, at the kitchen table while his mother watched something querulous on the news. The pamphlet did stonewall, a little, in the way pamphlets do, burying the useful sentence between a paragraph about fees and a paragraph about identity theft. But the sentence was there, and he copied it into his notebook like a formula: pay the full balance by the due date each month, and you avoid interest on new purchases. He sat with it for a while. The card wasn't free money and it wasn't a trap, exactly. It was a machine that ran on a deadline, and the deadline was the whole game.

The amp was still in the window on Friday. Delaney stood beside him looking at it, having ridden her bike across town for reasons she declined to state.

"Two hundred and thirty," Austin said.

"You have two hundred and thirty."

"I have sixty-six, and a plan involving a card." He explained it: buy nothing else, put the amp on the card, pay the whole thing off when his paycheck cleared on the ninth, before the due date, so the interest never even started. "It's not borrowing, really. It's borrowing for three weeks for free, if you do it right."

"That's a lot of ifs."

"That's the whole thing," he said. "The ifs are the system."

Delaney looked at him, then at the amp, then at the credit union next door, where a clerk was taping a sign in the window about a new-member disbursement special. "My brother paid the minimum for a year on a four-hundred-dollar couch," she said. "He still talks about it. He calls it the couch that disenfranchised him, which is not what that word means, but emotionally he's right."

Austin laughed, and then stood there a minute longer, honest with himself about the part he hadn't said out loud: that paychecks had been late before, that the ninth was a guess, that his mother's drawer full of twenties probably started with somebody's confident plan. He walked into the credit union and asked for the paperwork.

"Parent's signature," the clerk said. "And a deposit."

Austin counted out the sixty-six, keeping ten back for the bus, and started filling in the blanks.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
Mason had been at the mall for eleven minutes before Danica arrived, which gave him enough time to change his mind three times about which bench to sit on. He had read somewhere that slouching made you look easygoing, so he was slouching, elaborately, like a boy who had never cared about anything, when she came through the sliding doors in a green jacket and spotted him instantly.

"You look like you're melting," she said.

"I'm relaxed," he said, and sat up.

They walked. That was the whole plan, such as it was: walk, look at things, maybe eat. At the fountain they stopped to throw coins, and Mason noticed that they had both leaned on the rim the same way, elbows down, weight on the left arm, and he felt a small absurd flare of hope about it, as if the symmetry meant something. He had heard Maxime talking about this in the cafeteria last week, something Maxime had read for a psychology elective. Mason had been half listening, half defending his fries, and what he'd caught was this: in a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Maxime had demonstrated on Danica, of all people, copying the way she held her pen until she asked him why he was being weird, which had rather ruined the demonstration.

Now, walking beside Danica past the window of a shoe store, Mason thought about it seriously for the first time. If she had leaned like him without noticing, that was supposedly a good sign, or at least it meant she liked him, or at least it had meant that in a lab in 1999. But the logic turned slippery when he gripped it. If he deliberately leaned like her, and she never noticed, would she like him more? Was that a trick, or just effort? Every date involved a kind of performance, everyone knew that, everyone picked the good shirt and laughed a little harder at the easy jokes. But there was a line somewhere, and he could not see it.

He tested it, cautiously. When she tucked her hands into her jacket pockets, he tucked his into his, two seconds later, and watched her face for a change. She was telling him about her older brother, who had been home from college for a month and had turned virulent on the subject of their parents' grocery habits, complaining about everything with an enthusiasm that seemed to feed itself. "He's like a war now," she said. "You can't mention cereal without casualties." Mason laughed, genuinely, and his hands came out of his pockets again because he'd forgotten the experiment.

In the food court she got a lemonade and he got the same, though he had wanted a Coke, and they took a table by the railing overlooking the lower floor. He mirrored her again at intervals: chin on fist, then both forearms on the table, then the way she turned her cup by its handle in a slow circle. He was so busy tracking her posture that he missed most of a story about Mr. Ortiz, her chemistry teacher, who had granted the whole class clemency on a late lab report after the fire drill chaos, and she had to say "are you even listening" before he rewound and caught the thread. He apologized. He felt like a spy who was bad at spying, and worse, a dishonest one, because the compliment he wanted to give her was about her laugh and instead he was busy borrowing her elbows.

"You keep doing what I do," Danica said.

Mason felt his ears go hot. "What?"

"Like, when I moved my cup, you moved yours. When I leaned back you leaned back." She wasn't angry. She was looking at him with her head tilted, the way you look at a puzzle with one piece missing. "It's fine. It's just noticeable."

He considered lying, and the lie assembled itself quickly, something about stiff shoulders, and he let it fall apart. "Okay. There's this thing Maxime told me. A study, from 1999, these researchers, Tanya Charlund, no, Chartrand, and John Bargh. They found people liked a partner more when the partner mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. So I was, kind of, trying it." The confession sat on the table between them next to the two lemonades.

Danica was quiet long enough for the fountain downstairs to finish a whole cycle of its recorded music. Then she said, "So the whole point is that it only works when you don't notice."

"Yeah."

"And I noticed."

"Yeah," Mason said. He turned his cup by its handle, one slow circle, and this time it wasn't mimicry, it was just his hands needing something to do. "I also got lemonade instead of a Coke, if you want the full confession."

"That's the saddest thing I've ever heard," she said, but she was smiling, and she slid her cup an inch toward the middle of the table, and Mason, after a moment, slid his to meet it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
Aiden found the box on the top shelf of the hall closet while looking for his gown, which his mother swore she had hung on the back of the laundry room door and which, characteristically, was nowhere. The box was labeled in his grandfather's cramped hand: TAXES, DO NOT OPEN, which obviously meant open it. Inside, under a folder of receipts, lay a folded paper with a blue seal, and Aiden sat down on the closet floor right there among the winter boots to read it.

It was a diploma, sort of. Not a diploma exactly. It said something about a General Educational Development certificate, awarded to his grandfather in 1947, and Aiden had to read the header twice because he had assumed, his whole life, that his grandfather had finished high school. There had been a story about a championship baseball team. There had been a story about a chemistry teacher who let him light things on fire. He had told those stories at his own graduation party two weeks ago, holding a plastic cup, feeling like the heir to something.

"Saige is here," his mother called from the kitchen. Aiden slid the paper into the back pocket of his jeans, which was a decision he made without exactly deciding it, and went downstairs.

Saige was at the counter eating cereal out of the box, which she did at his house and at no one else's. Georgia came in behind her, still in her work polo from the pharmacy, smelling faintly of hand sanitizer. The three of them were supposed to be assembling a cooler for the lake that afternoon, the last plan of the last summer, though the plan had a loose, unenforced quality, like everything since graduation.

"Where's the gown?" Saige asked. "You're supposed to return it Monday."

"Lost. Sacrificed to the gods of the laundry room." Aiden got ice from the freezer and packed it awkwardly, too much in one end. He could feel the paper against the backs of his thighs when he bent over, a small stiff rectangle of correction.

"Your grandpa got his diploma, right?" Georgia said later, on the porch, because he had finally shown them, in the way you show something you pretend is casual. She was squinting at the certificate, holding it out of the direct sun. "My mom said he was in the army."

"He was," Aiden said. "But this isn't a diploma." He had looked it up on his phone in the bathroom, which was not a proud venue for research but an effective one. "It's a GED. They created the tests in 1942, for service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school. So they could show they had the skills anyway. He got out in '47 and took it then."

Saige lowered her sunglasses. "So all those stories."

"Were about his friend's school, probably. Or a school he went to before he enlisted. Or invented." He heard how bitter it came out and adjusted. "He never actually said he graduated. I said he graduated. I told everyone at the party."

They were quiet on the porch, the boreal light coming through the pines at the back of the lot, sharper than June should have been. Georgia handed the certificate back. "You could be mad," she said, "or you could notice he passed the tests after fighting a war. Which one of us has done either?"

"I'm not mad," Aiden said, and this was where his own narration failed him, because he was something, and mad was the nearest word on the shelf though not the right one. He was seventeen and had just been handed a piece of paper proving that the man he'd built his origin story around had left school at sixteen, and that the leaving had not been the end of anything. That was the part that sat wrong. He'd been walking around for years thinking of graduation as a door that closed behind you, and his grandfather had apparently gone through a different door entirely, a provisional one, invented in 1942 for people the regular door had failed.

At the lake, the cooler floated in the shallows because no one had put a rock in it. Saige waded out to retrieve it, cursing the cold, and Aiden sat on the dock with his sneakers off, thinking about the way Ms. Dang, his English teacher, had once told him not to pathologize every narrator who lied to him. "Some of them are just wrong," she'd said, "the way people are wrong, without malice." He'd written that in the margin of his notebook and felt superior about it. Now his grandfather was the narrator, dead four years, unavailable for cross-examination, wrong in a way that might have been malice or might have been shame or might have been a kind of courtesy, letting a boy believe in a chemistry teacher who permitted fires.

Georgia dropped down beside him, dripping. "You're doing the face," she said.

"I'm doing thinking. It's different."

"Is it, phonetically?" Saige called from the water, which wasn't even the right use of the word, but Aiden laughed anyway, the laugh cracking something loose. He took the certificate out of his pocket and folded it along its old creases, and it occurred to him that he would keep it in the box, or maybe in his own room, or maybe he would tell the story truthfully from now on, and he honestly did not know which, and that not knowing felt like the first adult thing he'd done all summer.

"Hey," he said. "Can either of you drive a stick? Because my mom's car is a stick and I just remembered I never learned."

Saige wrung out her shirt and climbed onto the dock. "I'll teach you for the rest of the ice."

Aiden held out the last cold can.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
The planetarium smelled like dust and lemon polish, and Alexis had the projector remote in his fist like a torch he wasn't sure how to switch on. Student night was in six days, and each of them had to stand under the dome and explain something real to an audience of parents and younger kids. He had chosen greenhouse gases because the topic felt important in a way he couldn't quite articulate, and because Mr. De Vries had approved it with a single nod, which somehow meant more than a paragraph of praise.

He was alone in the dome after school, running his slides. On the curved ceiling, the graph of carbon dioxide from Mauna Loa stretched across a century, climbing and climbing, but serrated along its length, jagged with little teeth, up and down, up and down. He frowned at it. If he stood up there and showed that, some kid would ask why the line wobbled, and the honest answer in his head was that instruments glitch, probably, that no measurement was perfect. That answer felt thin. He wrote a note to himself in the margin of his script: smooth it out? Nobody would notice.

Behind him, the door hinge complained, and Wesley came in carrying two paper cups of hot chocolate, one of which he set down beside Alexis's laptop without being asked. Wesley had been off school for three weeks with mono and had only just started to convalesce, pale and careful, moving like someone carrying a full glass. He still showed up. Alexis slid over to make room on the bench.

"What's the saw blade?" Wesley said, nodding at the dome.

"Machine noise," Alexis said. "I'm going to average it out."

Wesley sipped his drink and looked at the graph for a long moment, the way he looked at chess boards. "Every year, though. Same size teeth, every single year. Machines don't get tired on a schedule." He tilted his head. "What happens to trees in spring?"

"Leaves come out."

"And in fall?"

Alexis opened his mouth and then didn't say anything. The graph hung above them, its teeth suddenly legible, like footprints that had been there the whole time. Every spring and summer, northern plants breathed the gas in as they grew. Every autumn and winter, the dying leaves let it back out. The planet inhaling and exhaling, scribbled onto a century of data. "The wiggles are real," he said slowly. "The whole Northern Hemisphere, breathing."

"You're welcome," Wesley said, and stole the remote to put the stars on.

Alexis didn't smooth the graph. He rebuilt the presentation around the teeth, and by Thursday he had a new problem: Blaine, who was doing black holes and who found the whole idea of student night embarrassing. "It's a platitude, is what it is," Blaine said in the corridor, leaning against the trophy case. "'Save the planet,' the little kids clap, everyone feels great, nobody changes anything. You're doing a sermon with a graph."

"Then ask me a hard question," Alexis said. "Friday. Under the dome. In front of everyone. If my explanation falls apart, it falls apart."

His mother couldn't come on Friday. She had been convalescing since the surgery in March, and the doctors wanted her resting, not sitting in a cold dome for two hours. On Thursday night she left a note on his desk, in her narrow, looping hand, which he found before bed. Alexis, it began. I know you'd rather I were in the third row. When you get nervous, look for the exit sign like I taught you, and pretend I'm standing under it. Your father says the planetarium was where I told him I'd marry him, so the place owes us one good evening. Explain it slowly, the breathing part twice. Not everyone has a Wesley. Love, Mum. He read it twice and put it in his shirt pocket, a vestigial habit from primary school, notes for a lunchbox he no longer carried.

Friday, the dome filled. Mr. De Vries dimmed the stars so that only the graph glowed overhead, that long rising line with its faithful teeth. Alexis found the exit sign, green and steady, and began. He explained how the gases let sunlight through and held the heat, and when he reached the wiggles he made the audience breathe with him, in through spring, out through autumn, and a row of eleven-year-olds did it, fogging nothing, feeling something. Then Blaine's hand went up near the back.

"You said the yearly wiggles are the plants breathing," Blaine said. "Fine. But the line still goes up every year, higher than the year before. If the planet breathes in, why doesn't it ever breathe all of it back out?"

The dome was silent except for the projector fan. Alexis looked at the exit sign, then at the climbing line, then at Wesley, who was smiling into his cup and offering nothing, because the question was honest and it was his to answer. "I don't know all of why," Alexis said. "Partly I do. But the part I can't explain yet, I'd rather say that than invent something pretty." Blaine nodded once, slow, and lowered his hand, and after the lights came up he was the first one standing, walking up the aisle toward the stage.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: ProPublica, founded in 2007 as a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations, became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 2010.
story:
The notification woke Eve at 11:47, and by midnight the group chat had forty-one messages. She lay in bed with the screen six inches from her face, the blue light staining the ceiling, and scrolled up to find the beginning. Genesis had posted a screenshot of the school paper's budget: advertising revenue down again, the print edition probably cancelled after December. Beneath it she'd written, "we should just ask people for money like NPR."

Aleena replied first, as she always did, from her kitchen according to the photo she sent of her hand holding tea beside a bag of chips. "donations are their own kind of influence. rich people donate. then you owe rich people."

"advertisers are rich people too," Genesis typed. "we already owe them."

Eve sat up. Outside her window the streetlight buzzed, a moth ticking against the glass, and she typed nothing for a while, watching the three dots appear and vanish under Aleena's name. The paper was the one thing at school she'd claimed outright. She'd written about the cafeteria contract in October, and the company that held the contract had pulled its ads the following week. Mr. Banerjee, the adviser, had called it a coincidence in his nonchalant way, shrugging with one shoulder while he stapled the November layout together, and neither of them had mentioned it again.

She typed, "brb," and opened her laptop on the floor, cross-legged, the fan humming against her knee. She searched "newsroom funded by donations" and found a thing called ProPublica. Founded in 2007, a nonprofit newsroom funded by donations. In 2010 it became the first online news source to win a Pulitzer Prize. She read the sentence twice, then typed it into the chat with the link, following it with, "so it can work."

Aleena's reply came fast. "nonprofit doesn't mean no strings. someone still owns the servers lol."

"nobody owns it, that's the point of nonprofit," Genesis wrote. "no owner, no shareholders. readers fund it."

"readers with agendas fund it."

Eve got up and went to the kitchen for water. The floor was cold through her socks; the fridge made its small night sounds, clicking and settling. She stood at the counter holding the glass and thought about the cafeteria story, the way the ads had vanished like a tide going out, quietly, deniably. An advertiser didn't have to tell you what to write. The absence of money did the telling. She carried the glass back to her room, set it on the desk beside a stack of college brochures she was supposed to be narrowing down, and typed, "ok but here's the thing. ads are an externality we already live with. the paper attacked the cafeteria company and the money left. that already happened. donations are a different risk, not a new one."

Aleena sent a single "?".

"an externality," Eve typed. "a cost of something that falls on other people. the paper's independence is a cost of taking ad money, and we pay it without noticing."

Silence in the chat for a full minute, the timestamps staring at her. Then Genesis: "did you just define a word in the group chat."

"mr. banerjee used it in econ and I liked it, sue me."

"He would love this conversation btw," Aleena wrote. "should we just ask him?"

"not to decide for us," Eve typed, and then deleted it, and then retyped it, and sent it anyway. "not to decide for us."

The next morning they found him in the journalism room before first period, the smell of toner and old coffee, the December layouts spread across the back table. Genesis explained the idea with her phone flat between two mugs. Mr. Banerjee listened with his arms folded, looking at the mock-up of page one rather than at either of them.

"You could try it," he said finally. "A donor drive. Twenty dollars from families instead of ads." He straightened a corner of the layout that didn't need straightening. "The principal approves fund requests, you understand. Anything labeled a donation becomes his business."

"That's not ownership either," Eve said. "That's just scrutiny."

"It's a kind of string," he said. "Every structure has them. Your job is to choose which strings you can see."

Aleena, on her way in late with her bag half off her shoulder, caught the last exchange and stopped in the doorway. "So we don't know," she said. "That's your whole answer? We don't know?"

Eve looked at the page one mock-up, the headline she'd written about the cafeteria still holding its place, and found she wasn't embarrassed by the not-knowing. It sat beside the facts like another fact. She pulled out her phone and opened the chat, thumb hovering.

"Meeting Thursday," she typed. "Everyone brings one string they can live with."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In Darley and Latané's 1968 experiment, about 85 percent of people who thought they alone heard someone having a seizure helped, but only about 31 percent did when they thought four others heard it.
story:
Landon set his fork down before he started talking, which his mother recognized as a sign that whatever came next had been rehearsed on the drive home. "Something happened at the coffee shop today," he said. "A man collapsed near the counter. He was shaking. I think it was a seizure."

His father lowered his glass slowly. "Did you call anyone?"

"Deegan called 911. He was closer. But I want to tell you the weird part." Landon pushed a piece of chicken to the edge of his plate. "There were maybe ten people in there, and for the first few seconds nobody moved. Everybody looked at everybody else. This woman kept glancing at the barista like it was her job, and the barista looked at us, and Deegan just went. He was the only one."

The mother asked whether the man was all right, and Landon said the paramedics took him out on a stretcher, awake, talking, probably fine. Then, because Ms. Cohen had covered it in his social science elective last spring, he tried to contextualize what he'd seen, laying the afternoon over the textbook like tracing paper. "In 1968 these researchers, Darley and Latané, ran an experiment," he said. "People heard what sounded like someone having a seizure over a speaker. When each person thought they alone heard it, about 85 percent went for help. When they thought four other people also heard it, only about 31 percent did."

His father frowned. "That's the opposite of what you'd expect. More people, more help."

"Except people were certain someone else would go. That's what today felt like. I was third in line and I thought, the barista has a phone, the woman by the window is closer. I thought it for maybe four seconds. It felt like reasoning. Deegan later said it felt like nothing, he just went."

The salad bowl sat between them, untouched now. Landon's mother said that people weren't bad, they were afraid of doing it wrong, and his father said that was a generous reading, and for a while the conversation took the shape it always took, each of them defending a version of human nature the way other families argued about politics. Landon mostly listened. He was thinking about trade-offs, about how his four seconds of calculation had probably cost nothing because Deegan existed, and how the same calculation spread across a whole room had cost the man on the floor his first four seconds of help. His economics teacher called that an unintended consequence. His father called it entropy, the way systems drift toward disorder unless someone puts energy in, though he said it about the garage usually, not crowds.

"Here's the twist," Landon said. "Deegan didn't do it for the man. I found out after. He'd been trying to get the barista's attention for ten minutes to complain about his drink, and he was already halfway to the counter when the guy went down. He just happened to be moving."

His mother laughed, then covered it. "So the hero of the story wanted a refund."

"Or a remake. He was very specific." Landon smiled, but he kept going, because he'd been turning something over since the ambulance left. "It doesn't ruin it, though. That's what I can't decide. Ms. Cohen would say the outcome is what matters. My dad would say the motive matters. And I keep thinking it's both and neither, because if Deegan had been standing next to me, doing what I did, thinking what I thought, that man waits longer. Maybe a lot longer. Thirty-one percent longer, kind of."

His father pointed his fork at him. "You're not responsible for a room."

"I'm not sure that's true. I'm responsible for the part of the room I am." Landon heard how it sounded, like a poster in a guidance office, and he dialed it back. "I don't mean it that grand. I mean next time I'll know my first move is probably to do nothing, and knowing that might be worth something. Or it might be deleterious in some way I can't see yet. Maybe I'll hesitate differently, second-guessing my second-guessing."

They finished eating mostly in quiet after that. His mother cleared the plates and stacked them wrong, tureens on top of saucers, and the pile slid a centimeter and held. His father dried. Landon filled three glasses with water even though nobody asked, because the pitcher was full and near his elbow and it seemed, tonight, like the kind of thing a person should just do without checking whether someone else would.

Later, drying his hands on his jeans, he texted Deegan: did you ever get your drink remade. The reply came back a minute later: she comped it. whole thing. then the man's daughter came in later and hugged the barista by mistake. Landon read it twice, set the phone face down, and carried the garbage out to the bin, where the lid was heavy with rainwater and he had to lift it with both hands.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election.
story:
The town hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Emma sat in the third row with a cue card she had rewritten four times, each version smaller than the last. The issue was simple enough to fit on a flyer: the youth council wanted the power to remove its own chair between elections, and the councillor who ran the meeting had agreed, reluctantly, to let the public speak. Felix-Antoine had signed her up for a slot without asking, which was either friendship or sabotage, and Bruce had spent the bus ride arguing that the whole thing was pointless because a recall rule would never actually be used.

"Everything is never used until it is," Emma said, and Bruce rolled his eyes, and that was the end of the conversation until Mr. MacLeod, two rows ahead, turned around.

"You're the one speaking on the removal clause?" he asked. He had taught her Grade Nine geography and now he showed up at meetings like this the way other retired men showed up at fishing holes. "Then you might want the number I keep in my head. On the twenty-eighth of March, 1979, the government of James Callaghan in the United Kingdom fell to a vote of no confidence. The count was 311 to 310. One vote. It forced a general election."

Emma wrote it down, the pen pressing so hard it tore the card a little. "Vote of no confidence," she repeated, and he nodded, satisfied, and turned back around before she could ask him anything else.

When her name was called, she stood and found that her mouth was dry in a way no amount of water would have fixed. The room held maybe sixty people, which in a town of this size meant everyone who mattered and several people who just liked chairs. "You're proposing that we can remove a chair we elected," she began. "I used to think that was dishonest. You voted, you live with it. That's how we pick a prime minister or a president, right, except it isn't, not exactly." She heard Felix-Antoine shift behind her and steadied herself on the edge of the podium. "A president gets a fixed term. You cannot remove a president mid-term for losing support, only for incapacitating himself or breaking the law, and even then it takes forever. A prime minister can be toppled by the same parliament that put him there. In 1979 the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence, 311 to 310, and that single vote forced a general election."

A man near the back, the one who sold insurance and called into the local radio show with opinions about technocracy, stood up to object. "That's Britain," he said. "We don't need their procedures. Next you'll tell us the councillors should resign over a pothole."

"I'm not saying we import their whole system," Emma said, and here she was inventing as she went, feeling her way across the gap between the two ways of doing things. "I'm saying the principle is different. A president is like a lock you can't open until the timer runs out. A prime minister holds power only as long as the room keeps confidence in him. If we're a council and not a technocracy of people who know better than us, then the chair should be answerable to us the way a prime minister is, not untouchable the way a president is." She paused. "The difference isn't which one is nicer. It's what happens when trust runs out. One system waits. The other one counts."

The insurance man muttered something noxious about teenagers and parliamentary fantasies, and a few people laughed, but the councillor at the front had stopped shuffling his papers and was looking at her with actual attention, which frightened her more than the laughter had. Bruce gave her a thumbs up so exaggerated it was almost sarcastic, and she sat down before her knees could register what had happened.

The vote came at the end of the evening, after an hour of potholes and a drainage dispute nobody fully understood. The councillor read the amendment aloud, then asked for a show of hands, and the room went quiet in the way that makes you hear the ventilation. Emma counted along with everyone else and lost her place twice. It did not come out 311 to 310; it came out 17 to 15, with two abstentions and one hand that rose halfway and then dropped, and for a moment nobody was sure whether to count the halfway hand. The councillor looked at it, looked at the chair of the youth council, who had argued against her own vulnerability all evening with a tight, careful voice, and then said, "Carried."

Felix-Antoine grabbed her sleeve in the aisle. "Two votes. You were two votes away from nothing." Emma looked down at her cue card, at the torn place where the pen had gone through, at the numbers Mr. MacLeod had given her, 311 and 310, sitting there next to 17 and 15 like they were comparing notes. Mr. MacLeod was putting on his coat by the door, and she pushed through the folding chairs toward him, still holding the card.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Anthony had eleven dollars, two tickets to the homecoming game, and a folding chair under each arm, which he hoped did not look as penurious as it felt. Faith had suggested the game herself, which he took as a good sign, or at least as a sign better than silence. He had exactly two hours until her mother's curfew at ten, a fact he had written on his hand in pen and then sweated partially into the number eight.

She was waiting by the gate in a denim jacket, and she waved before he had decided whether waving first would seem desperate. They found seats on the visitors' side because it was emptier, and because Anthony wanted room to set down the drinks, which he had bought with most of the eleven dollars. He carried them like a man carrying acid across a laboratory.

The marching band was still on the field when it happened. Faith reached for her cup at the same moment he angled it toward her, and the lid caught, and the whole thing went over in a long brown arc onto her jacket, her jeans, the folding chair, and one clarinet player's abandoned music folder. She stood up fast, which only spread it, and her face did the thing faces do when someone is calculating how much of an evening can still be salvaged. "Great," she said. "Great. Two minutes in and I'm the disaster."

Anthony's first instinct was to insist otherwise at high volume, but he had spent the previous weekend reading a psychology article he'd found while avoiding a history essay, and something in it surfaced now like a cork. "There was this experiment," he said, dabbing her sleeve with the napkins he had, in a rare act of foresight, brought. "Nineteen sixty-six. Elliot Aronson and his colleagues. A quiz contestant who was really competent spilled a cup of coffee, and people rated him more likable afterward."

Faith stopped wiping her jeans. "More likable. For spilling."

"For spilling. They call it the pratfall effect." He handed her the last napkin. "So statistically, you just became the best part of this date."

She looked at him for a second, and then she laughed, a real one, loud enough that a man two rows down turned around. "Did you study for this? Did you study for me?"

"No," said Anthony, who absolutely had, in the sense that he had read everything he could find about first dates at two in the morning. He had approached the evening the way his father approached an argument, like an ideologue with a binder of evidence, certain that if he knew enough rules nothing could go wrong. The spill had emancipated him from that almost immediately. There was something freeing about watching the plan fail in the first two minutes, something he did not want to examine too closely in case it fell apart under inspection.

They went to the concession stand so she could rinse the jacket, and the walk took them behind the end zone where the band was assembling, and Faith, still coffee-stained and laughing, started telling him about her younger brother, who had once set fire to a marshmallow in their microwave twice in one week. Anthony bought her a hot chocolate with his remaining three dollars and a quarter he found in his pocket, and he understood that the pratfall effect was probably about the competent person, specifically, which meant it applied to her, not to him, and he could not decide whether that was reassuring or just another rule he would get wrong.

The score was 14 to 7 when the fourth quarter started and her mother texted that she'd be there at nine thirty, half an hour earlier than the pen-written eight. Faith showed him the phone with an expression of theatrical despair. "So much for the two-hour plan."

"It was a good plan," Anthony said. "It survived contact with reality for almost a full cup of coffee."

They stayed until the clock ran down anyway, standing at the fence, and when the home team kicked the winning field goal the crowd noise arrived at them like weather. Faith grabbed his sleeve, coffee stain and all, and jumped up and down. In the parking lot, under the one working light, her mother's car idled at the curb.

"Okay," Faith said, one hand on the door handle. "Next time, you spill something."

"Next time?"

She was already halfway into the car. "Pratfall effect," she called through the window. "Look it up."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
The book club met in the back room of the library, where Mr. Munro set out folding chairs in a circle and left a plate of biscuits nobody touched until the last ten minutes. Brooke arrived early with her copy of Jane Eyre and a spiral notebook, and she took the chair beside the window so she could see the car park, though there was nothing to see in it but Tyler's mother's hatchback and a row of drying hedges.

They had read Volume One, Chapters One through Six, and the plan was simply to talk. But Brooke had spent the week before with a page of notes from a lecture she'd found online, half-watched on her phone while drying her hair, about reading old novels through a Marxist lens. She hadn't understood all of it. What she'd caught was a single question that kept repeating itself in her head afterward, and she had decided, in a vague and slightly stubborn way, that tonight she would find out whether the question could survive contact with an actual chapter.

The question, the lecturer had said, was this: whose labour makes these comfortable lives possible? She had written it on the first page of the notebook and then, on the train of some instinct, made two columns underneath. In one column she had counted every time a servant was named in the six chapters. In the other, every time a servant spoke.

When the circle had settled, Mr. Munro opened with something about the red-room and whether it was frightening or symbolic, and Mikaela said it was obviously both, and Tyler argued that making everything symbolic drained the actual fear out of it, that a ten-year-old locked in a room where her uncle died doesn't need the room to mean something. Brooke let this go on for a while, watching the words in her notebook, until she realized that if she waited any longer she would talk herself out of it entirely.

"I counted something," she said, and immediately wished she'd phrased it differently, because everyone turned. She turned the notebook around. "In these chapters. The servants, Bessie and Miss Abbot and the others. They're named fourteen times. And they speak, I mean actually speak, four times. And two of those four are them telling Jane to be quiet."

"That's a lot of counting," Tyler said, but not unkindly.

"A Marxist reading," Brooke went on, feeling her way, "asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible. And the weird thing is, the novel does mention the servants. They're there, carrying things, lighting fires, doing up buttons. Mrs. Reed's whole morning exists because someone else made it exist. But they only pass by. The book notices them exactly as much as Mrs. Reed does." She heard herself speeding up and made herself slow. "I don't know if Brontë meant that. I don't know if you can mean something you don't seem to see."

Mikaela leaned forward. "So are you saying Brontë's blind or that the blindness is the point?"

"That's the part I can't decide. Because if it's the point, then Jane being poor and dependent isn't just her problem, it's her position in a system, and the servants are one rung below her and she barely registers them either. Jane hates being degraded by Mrs. Reed, and then she goes home and Bessie laces her boots." Brooke had not planned to say that sentence; she heard it arrive and was slightly startled by it.

Mr. Munro, who had been listening with his hands folded, started to speak, and Brooke tensed, ready for the correction. But all he said was, "Does anyone want to answer Mikaela's question?" and turned the circle back to them, and Brooke understood that this was the whole gift of him, that he would not settle it.

Tyler tried. "Maybe it's like this," he said. "You can externalize the system, make it a thing outside the characters, a machine they're all stuck in. Or you can say the characters are the system, that Jane's small blindnesses are how the machine runs. Those aren't the same reading. The first one lets everyone off a bit. The second one is harsher and probably truer."

"But you can't fully know an author's intent," Mikaela said. "It stays open."

"Then it stays open," Brooke said, and found she didn't mind. There had been an injunction in her head all week, something like an order from the exam board of her own imagination: take a position, defend it, conclude. The position she actually had was more like a room with two doors, and she was beginning to suspect that living there, in the uncertainty, was what the counting had been for. She was even starting to wonder whether the certainty Tyler offered, his either-or, was just an extrinsic frame laid over the novel to make it easier to grade, a scaffolding that had nothing to do with the building.

They talked for another twenty minutes, and then the biscuits finally went around, and Mr. Munro collected the chairs while Mikaela argued that Jane Eyre was secretly funny and Tyler denied it. Brooke stacked her notebook and her novel on top of each other and realized, with a small flush of pleasure, that next month's chapters were the ones at Lowood School, where Jane would be fed by cooks she'd never be introduced to and taught by teachers who worked for nothing.

She was the last one out. At the door, Mr. Munro was wiping the biscuit crumbs off the table with a cloth, and he nodded at her notebook and said, "I'll need to put the chairs away before I lock up."

Dylan slid his tray along the counter, waiting while the barista steamed milk for the man ahead of him, and tried to work out how to say what he wanted to say without sounding like a management consultant. Shreya had already claimed the corner table by the window, her laptop open, a pencil behind her ear like a carpenter. Darren arrived late, out of breath, carrying nothing.

"I need advice," Dylan said, sitting. "It's my brother. He leaves dishes everywhere, shoes in the hallway, wet towels on his bed, which, how does that even work. So I had this idea. I pay him. A dollar a chore. I figured he'd want the money."

Darren unwrapped a straw from someone else's pile of napkins. "You'd be out like ten bucks a week."

"Ten bucks a week for a hallway you can actually walk down. That's a trade-off I'd take." He said the word deliberately, the way Mr. Villanueva had said it in seminar that morning, weighing it like a coin. Responsibility, trade-offs, consequences. He'd been carrying the words around all day, testing them against his own life the way you tap a wall to find the stud.

Shreya lowered the pencil from her ear. "Okay, but my mom has this story about exactly this. Hanoi, 1902. The French colonial authorities ran the city, and they had a rat problem, so they paid a bounty for each rat tail people brought in." She drew a quick rat in the margin of her notes, long tail, absurd ears. "So what do you think happened?"

Darren squinted at the drawing. "They caught all the rats."

"People started cutting off the tails and letting the rats go, so the rats could breed. The rat problem grew." She tapped the pencil twice against the page. "My mom tells it at the dinner table whenever anyone proposes paying anyone for anything. My sister suggested paying our brother per chore and got the whole Hanoi lecture."

"Your mom tells rat stories at dinner," Darren said, "and you think my family's weird."

Dylan was only half listening. He was thinking about his brother holding a pair of kitchen scissors over a live rat, calculating, and finding it obvious. Not evil. Obvious. The bounty paid for tails, not for dead rats, so a rational person in Hanoi kept rats alive, kept them breeding, because a dead rat was a rat that couldn't earn you anything tomorrow. The incentive and the goal had come apart from each other, quietly, and nobody in the administration had noticed until the tails piled up and the streets were worse than before. Unintended consequences, he thought; the words felt less like vocabulary now and more like a thing with a smell.

"So pay per outcome," he said slowly. "Not per chore. Like, a dollar for a clean hallway, whatever it takes to get there. Then he can't farm it." But even as he said it, he heard the seam in the plan, because a clean hallway could be faked too, dirt swept under the couch, dishes rinsed and not washed, and did he really want to become his brother's inspector, patrolling the hallway every night with a checklist? He tried to hold both ideas at once, the way Mr. Villanueva had shown them with the trolley diagrams: the pragmatic view, where you pick the lever that moves the outcome you want, and the older view, where his brother was a person, ten years old, with some flickering sentience of his own, not a system to be tuned. Maybe the chores weren't really about the chores. Maybe they were about belonging to a household. He didn't know. He was honest with himself about that part: he didn't know.

"That's why my mom hates the whole framework," Shreya said. "You start thinking people are rats."

"I'm not bellicose about it," Dylan said. "I just want to find my shoes."

The argument invigorated him more than the coffee had, and they stayed another forty minutes, sketching plans on napkins, tearing them up, the pile of torn napkins growing in the middle of the table like something they'd have to clean up themselves.

When they finally left, Dylan walked home and found his brother in the kitchen, standing over the sink, actually washing a dish. He felt a flash of triumph before he saw the notebook on the counter, open to a page of tally marks, forty-one of them, in careful pencil columns. "Dad's paying me a quarter a chore now," his brother said, soaping the same fork for the third time. "Does drying count as a separate one?"
